messages.subject: STAN syntax - fixing parameters
messages.subject_clean: STAN syntax - fixing parameters
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm currently building a model to explain count data and am having a little difficulty with the STAN syntax.  I've attached the model, ToyModel.stan, and any help would be most appreciated.

1: How can I fix one element from a vector of parameter?

Initially I tried (attached as ToyModel1.stan) :
transformed parameters{
...
vector[NT] Beta;
Beta[1] <- 0;
...
}

However this leads to the following error:

Error : Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable[1]  is 1.#QNAN:0, but must not be nan!

error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

My work around for this was to specify a strong prior on the first element of the Beta vector which "works" but isn't an ideal solution, it also leads to another question about STAN's syntax.

Is it possible to put a prior on a slice of a vector?

So in this case it would be something like:

model{
...
Beta[2:NT] ~ normal(0,1)
...
}

Cheers,

Dominic

On 9/1/13 10:33 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Sunday, September 1, 2013 9:45:29 AM UTC-4, Dominic Edwards wrote:
>
>     1: How can I fix one element from a vector of parameter?
>

>     Initially I tried (attached as /ToyModel1.stan/) :

>
>     |
>     transformed parameters{
>     ...
>     vector[NT] Beta;
>     Beta[1] <- 0;
>     ...
>     }
>     |
>
>
> You want to declare the free elements in the parameters section and then copy them into a larger vector in the model
> section after specifying the fixed values. Then put the prior on the former. Like this
>
> |
> parameters {
>    vector[NT-1] Beta_free;
> }
> model {
>    vector[NT] Beta;
>    Beta[1] <- 0.0;
>    for (i in 1:(NT-1)) Beta[i+1] <- Beta_free[i];
>    Beta_free <- normal(0.0, 4.0);
>    ...
> }
> |
>
> In the next version of Stan, there is a tail() function which would allow you to write this without the explicit loop in
> the .stan file but either way it becomes a fast loop in the C++ code.

I'm afraid I don't have tail() [or head() or block()]
working as an lvalue (legal left side of assignment).

We could (a) write special block-assignment functions (easy), (b) figure
out how to do a better job with lvalues on the LHS (more challenging, at
least for me), or (c) cobble something together
like I did for rows of matrices using indexing (that is, if a is a matrix,
then a[n] is a row that's a valid lvalue).

I'd probably opt for (c) if it's an immediate need.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Refining normal distribution with one data point [R scalars vs. arrays]
messages.body_plain:
Ack.  No, it's because (a) we do error checking for shape on the
inputs, and (b) R conflates scalars and implicit arrays of length 1.
So if you do

    b <- c(17.2);

then R doesn't know if b is a length-1 array or a scalar.  The above
produces the same result in b as

    b <- 17.2;

Jiqiang provides a workaround here:

   https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/d-R7J6MldkQ

Bottom line is that instead of

    "b" = b

in a list, you need to use the array() function

    "b" = array(b, dim=length(b))

to convince R that the value for "b" in the list is an array.

Yet another gotcha we need to somehow call out in the doc
without being too distracting.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] About "simplex" command.-
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] About "simplex" command.-
messages.body_plain:
The exact transform used to map (K - 1) unconstrained
variables to a K-simplex is described in the transformations
chapter of the manual.

If you just declare a parameter as a simplex[K], then
its distribution is implicitly uniform over K-simplexes.
So yes, it's Dirichlet(1), where 1 is a unit K-vector, because
that's uniform on simplexes.

The sampling is carried out by adjusting for the Jacobian in the
tranform.

For instance, this model will just sample theta
uniformly at random from the space of valid K-simplexes:

   data {
     int<lower=2> K;
   parameters {
     simplex[K] theta;
   }
   model {
   }

You can then add in a prior, which is just multiplied into the
total log probability (the uniform multiplies by a constant, so
has no effect).  If you want to put a Dirichlet  prior on theta, do
it explicitly in the model, as in:

   model {
     theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
   }

where alpha is defined to be a non-negative K-vector in the data (or
hierarchically as a parameter).

- Bob

messages.subject: stan model I made after reading "Bayesian Model-Building by Pure Thought"
messages.subject_clean: stan model I made after reading "Bayesian Model-Building by Pure Thought"
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I was reading a paper <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/deep.pdf> that Andrew linked to in a recent post <http://andrewgelman.com/2013/08/19/bda3-still-i-hope-at-40-off-and-a-link-to-one-of-my-favorite-papers/>, about wanting models to be insensitive to the scale of discretization. As one example, he describes (section 3) fitting a function that's constrained to be increasing, and how you'll really be led astray by a prior that's uniform over the function values at discrete points (with a restriction that the values are increasing). As the number of points in the discretization increases, the mass of the prior concentrates around a straight line, which is bad.

Just for fun, I thought about how I might approach this problem, and then coded the model in Stan. I imagine that my approach is either wrong, or is old hat to you folks. But I'm writing to this group about it because:

1. I'm very new to Stan (etc.), so if anyone has any feedback (on either the Stan model or how I decided to think about the problem), I'd really appreciate it.
2. Maybe something here (the approach, the model, the R code) will be interesting or useful to one of you? I'm very new to Stan, so I don't know what's interesting vs. trivial to people.

So here's how I thought about it:

The function  mu  increases from 0 at time 0 to some unknown value at time 1, with discrete intermediate values  mu[i]  (where  i  represents the discretization and ranges from  1  to  N). Each data point  y[i]  is drawn from a normal distribution centered on  mu[i].

I modeled the jumps as chi-squared-distributed. This is nice since 1 jump that's distributed as chi-squared(k)  is then equivalent to  n  independent jumps that are distributed as  chi-squared(k/N). Then our prior for the function  mu  is independent of the scale of the discretization if we express it in terms of  k_0, where the sum of all the jumps (which is  mu[N]  ) is distributed as  chi-squared(k_0). Similarly, the variance of the  y's  should scale with  1/N, since I'm assuming that the  y's  at a coarser scale are an average of the y's at a finer scale.  So the model is:

(For i in 1:N):

mu_i ~ mu_{i-1} + s*chi_square(k_0/N)   (mu_0 = 0)
y_y ~ N(mu_i, sqrt(sigma_0_sq*N))

(The parameter  s  lets us vary both the size and variance of the jumps. Maybe it would have been better to express the model explicitly in terms of the jump size/variance independently.)

You can see my Stan code and R code on Github here <https://github.com/dchudz/misc/tree/master/stan%20models/increasing%20by%20chi%20square%20increments>.

In the plots (attached and on Github), you can see me doing what Andrew suggested in that paper: I fit the model (using simulated data) at two different levels of aggregation. The  y's  at the coarser scale are an average of the  y's  at the finer scale. Plotting the posterior means of  mu  for each model, we can see that the estimated function is similar for the two different discretizations, which is what we would hope for. I also plotted samples from the posterior from the two models, and they look pretty similar.

A better model (hierarchical) would (instead of assuming they're known) put a prior on the hyperparameters (k_0, s, sigma_0_sq). But I decided to start from here.

I'd love to hear what you think!

Thanks,

-David

On Sep 2, 2013, at 10:00 PM, David Chudzicki wrote:

> Hi everyone,
>
> I was reading a paper <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/deep.pdf> that Andrew linked to in a recent post <http://andrewgelman.com/2013/08/19/bda3-still-i-hope-at-40-off-and-a-link-to-one-of-my-favorite-papers/>, about wanting models to be insensitive to the scale of discretization. As one example, he describes (section 3) fitting a function that's constrained to be increasing, and how you'll really be led astray by a prior that's uniform over the function values at discrete points (with a restriction that the values are increasing). As the number of points in the discretization increases, the mass of the prior concentrates around a straight line, which is bad.
>
> Just for fun, I thought about how I might approach this problem, and then coded the model in Stan. I imagine that my approach is either wrong, or is old hat to you folks. But I'm writing to this group about it because:
>
> 1. I'm very new to Stan (etc.), so if anyone has any feedback (on either the Stan model or how I decided to think about the problem), I'd really appreciate it.
> 2. Maybe something here (the approach, the model, the R code) will be interesting or useful to one of you? I'm very new to Stan, so I don't know what's interesting vs. trivial to people.
>
> So here's how I thought about it:
>
> The function  mu  increases from 0 at time 0 to some unknown value at time 1, with discrete intermediate values  mu[i]  (where  i  represents the discretization and ranges from  1  to  N). Each data point  y[i]  is drawn from a normal distribution centered on  mu[i].
>
> I modeled the jumps as chi-squared-distributed. This is nice since 1 jump that's distributed as chi-squared(k)  is then equivalent to  n  independent jumps that are distributed as  chi-squared(k/N). Then our prior for the function  mu  is independent of the scale of the discretization if we express it in terms of  k_0, where the sum of all the jumps (which is  mu[N]  ) is distributed as  chi-squared(k_0). Similarly, the variance of the  y's  should scale with  1/N, since I'm assuming that the  y's  at a coarser scale are an average of the y's at a finer scale.  So the model is:
>
> (For i in 1:N):
>
> mu_i ~ mu_{i-1} + s*chi_square(k_0/N)   (mu_0 = 0)
> y_y ~ N(mu_i, sqrt(sigma_0_sq*N))
>
> (The parameter  s  lets us vary both the size and variance of the jumps. Maybe it would have been better to express the model explicitly in terms of the jump size/variance independently.)
>
> You can see my Stan code and R code on Github here <https://github.com/dchudz/misc/tree/master/stan%20models/increasing%20by%20chi%20square%20increments>.
>
> In the plots (attached and on Github), you can see me doing what Andrew suggested in that paper: I fit the model (using simulated data) at two different levels of aggregation. The  y's  at the coarser scale are an average of the  y's  at the finer scale. Plotting the posterior means of  mu  for each model, we can see that the estimated function is similar for the two different discretizations, which is what we would hope for. I also plotted samples from the posterior from the two models, and they look pretty similar.
>
> A better model (hierarchical) would (instead of assuming they're known) put a prior on the hyperparameters (k_0, s, sigma_0_sq). But I decided to start from here.
>
> I'd love to hear what you think!
>
> Thanks,
>
> -David

> The exact transform used to map (K - 1) unconstrained
> variables to a K-simplex is described in the transformations
> chapter of the manual.
>
> If you just declare a parameter as a simplex[K], then
> its distribution is implicitly uniform over K-simplexes.
> So yes, it's Dirichlet(1), where 1 is a unit K-vector, because
> that's uniform on simplexes.
>
> The sampling is carried out by adjusting for the Jacobian in the
> tranform.
>
> For instance, this model will just sample theta
> uniformly at random from the space of valid K-simplexes:
>
>   data {
>     int<lower=2> K;
>   parameters {
>     simplex[K] theta;
>   }
>   model {
>   }
>
> You can then add in a prior, which is just multiplied into the
> total log probability (the uniform multiplies by a constant, so
> has no effect).  If you want to put a Dirichlet  prior on theta, do
> it explicitly in the model, as in:
>
>   model {
>     theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
>   }
>
> where alpha is defined to be a non-negative K-vector in the data (or

>
> Uh oh.  Let's see if we can help.

Hi Tutor!
Seriously, I thank you a lot.

But I wish to say that Andrew Gelman ("Another option is to just ditch
the scaled-inverse-Wishart and use LKJ or something else") is likely
right ;-)
I've looked around and found this discussion:

https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-dev/21BZjOp1IAg/tOmUhMLKzmwJ

and a message by Ben Goodrich: "The {scaled, inverse} Wishart priors are
overly popular due to their computational convenience in Gibbs samplers,
but I suspect they are computationally inconvenient for HMC due to the
induced high dependence among parameters. Maybe NUTS 3 will make this
feasible, but it should already be feasible in NUTS 1 with an LKJ prior
and eta >= 1."

So replacing BUGS+Scaled-inverse-Wishart with Stan+LKJ could make sense
even when rewriting the ARM code...

I've tried to keep things as simple as possibile:
 > library(MASS)
 > N <- 1000 # or 10000 or...
 > Sigma <- matrix(c(10,3,3,2), 2, 2)
 > y <- mvrnorm(n=N, rep(0, 2), Sigma)

but all my Stan+Scaled-inverse-Wishart models were disappointing: slow
sampling, low ESS and high Rhat.
Even when I applied your suggestions, even the multidimensional Matth trick.

So I've tried:

data {
   int N;
   int K;
   vector[K] y[N];
}
parameters {
   vector[K] mu;
   vector<lower=0>[K] sd;
   corr_matrix[K] L;
}
transformed parameters {
   matrix[K,K] S;
   cov_matrix[K] Sigma;
   S <- diag_matrix(sd);
   Sigma <- S * L * S;
}
model {
   L ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
   for (n in 1:N)
     y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
}

No trick but LKJ.
Have I misundestood LKJ? Very likely!
But here are the results (N = 10000, iter=2000, not iter = \infty):

                 mean se_mean   sd       50% n_eff Rhat
mu[1]           0.05    0.00 0.03      0.05  2349    1
mu[2]           0.01    0.00 0.01      0.01  2342    1
sd[1]           3.19    0.00 0.02      3.19  2256    1
sd[2]           1.42    0.00 0.01      1.42  2424    1
L[1,1]          1.00    0.00 0.00      1.00  4000  NaN
L[1,2]          0.67    0.00 0.01      0.67  2297    1
L[2,1]          0.67    0.00 0.01      0.67  2297    1

S[1,1]          3.19    0.00 0.02      3.19  2256    1
S[1,2]          0.00    0.00 0.00      0.00  4000  NaN
S[2,1]          0.00    0.00 0.00      0.00  4000  NaN
S[2,2]          1.42    0.00 0.01      1.42  2424    1
Sigma[1,1]     10.15    0.00 0.15     10.15  2257    1

Sigma[2,1]      3.06    0.00 0.06      3.06  2051    1
Sigma[2,2]      2.03    0.00 0.03      2.03  2425    1
lp__       -22083.59    0.05 1.58 -22083.24   946    1

Faster sampling, reasonable means/medians, ESSs, and Rhats (as to those
NaNs, they come from a division by a zero variance when the "parameter"
is a constant, don't they?)

I'ld like such a solution.

Sergio

PS:

>> I must say that I don't understand well how statements in the
>> transformed parameters block work.
>
> Have you read the manual language sections on transformed parameters?
>
> In a nutshell, all of the data, transformed data, and parameters are
> available when you compute transformed parameters, which will then be
> available in the model.
>
>> For instance, may I define a[j] as xi_a * B_raw[j,1] when B_raw is not
>> yet defined, because it is modeled in the model
>> block?
>
> B_raw is declared in the parameters block, so it will be
> defined at the point the transformed parameter block is
> executed.  The sampling statmeents do NOT define the variables
> on their left side, they just increment the total log probability
> based on variables that already have to be defined.

This is what I was missing. Thanks!

OK, I now understand the model after waking up and reading the
reference you linked.  I rewrote the model and R code
to place more of the computation inside Stan.

You'll see if you look at the traceplots that theta converges
almost instantly [use: traceplot(fit,"theta") in R].

If you wanted, you could use the generated quantities block
and theta to generate samples for n.  Stan only dumps out
the unnormalized log probabilities, which I've coded up as
a transformed parameter.

produces --- Rao-Blackwell says it should be more efficient.  So I added code
to do the normalized dump of probablity of n given data, as well as posterior mean.
Posterior mode's also easy to calculate or view by inspection (it's 73).  So

messages.body_plain:
Even though it didn't turn out to be a problem in this particular application, I'm curious whether anyone has thoughts on the best/simplest way to resolve the sign indeterminacy (i.e., reflection invariance) of item-response models in Stan. For example, say you want to do so by constraining the discrimination parameter of one item to be positive. Assuming that the discriminations beta have to be declared as a vector (as in "vector<lower=0>[K] beta;"), would it make sense to then transform the relevant parameter (indexed by pos_indx) with something like the following?:

beta[pos_indx] <- abs(beta[pos_indx])

Or should the sign restriction be declared when the parameter is defined?

Thanks for your help!
~Devin

On Friday, October 12, 2012 5:26:32 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Friday, October 12, 2012 4:09:08 PM UTC-4, Josh Rosenau wrote:
> > Looks like ordered_logistic doesn't have a vectorized form, so I couldn't test the vectorized alternatives with that, but I did try it with the bernoulli_logit function.
> >
> > Just moving bernoulli_logit out of the loop using foo to hold the calculated vector did give a speed boost
>
> Yes, loops involving assignment statements ( <- ) only are cheap. Loops involving sampling statements ( ~ or lp__ <- lp__ + whatever; ) are expensive because they change the log-posterior. So, if you are able to use a vectorized distribution, it is often worthwhile to take the sampling statement out of the loop even if you have to do a loop with assignment statements to line up the parameters.
>
> Although Stan currently does not have an ordered_probit function, you might be able to recast your model like you would under a Gibbs sampler with data augmentation of a latent variable governed by the cutpoints. That would be a lot of effort to code (and might not work well), but in the end you would be able to vectorize the y_star ~ normal(mu, 1).
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
On 9/4/13 9:07 PM, Devin Caughey wrote:
> Even though it didn't turn out to be a problem in this particular application, I'm curious whether anyone has thoughts
> on the best/simplest way to resolve the sign indeterminacy (i.e., reflection invariance) of item-response models in
> Stan.

Using priors or fixing values is going to work best in Stan.

For a proper IRT model, there's no item coding uncertainty
like there is in ideal point models, so it makes the most sense
to me to constrain the discrimination parameter be to be positive.

> For example, say you want to do so by constraining the discrimination parameter of one item to be positive.
> Assuming that the discriminations beta have to be declared as a vector (as in "vector<lower=0>[K] beta;"), would it make
> sense to then transform the relevant parameter (indexed by pos_indx) with something like the following?:
>
> beta[pos_indx] <- abs(beta[pos_indx])

This is not a good idea because the indeterminacy is
still there in the underlying sampler.

Also, you can't technically reassign a parameter like this.
You'd have something like:

   beta[k] <- abs(beta_raw[k]);

The sampling is then actually done over beta_raw, which
has the non-identifiability.  It may not sound like this would
be a problem, but we're trying to do things like identify posterior
scales, which this messes with because the high mass area of
the posterior isn't contiguous.

In general, we prefer to make the underlying distribution
in the unconstrained parameters identified.  For the same
reason, I wouldn't recommend adjusting unidentified raw parameters
in some other way.  It might work, but it's making life hard
on sampler adaptation.

> Or should the sign restriction be declared when the parameter is defined?

Yes.  What really happens here is this:

   beta[k] <- exp(beta_raw[k]);

And in order to allow sampling to happen on beta_raw when the
model will be defined in terms of beta, we apply a Jacobian
adjustment (here just lp__ <- lp__ + beta_raw[k]).

> Thanks for your help!

But wait, there's more.  You also have scale identifiability and
additive offset identity.  So if you have student abilities
alpha[j], item difficulties beta[i], item discrimination
delta[i], then

   y[i,j] ~ bernoulli_logit( delta[i] * ( alpha[j] - beta[i] ) );

has three kinds of non-identifiability:

   1.  add to alpha and beta

   2.  multiply alpha and beta, divide delta

   3.  flip all signs

What I did in an IRT model I just fit was to take

    alpha ~ normal(0,1);     // identifying prior on abilities

    beta ~ normal(0,10);     // vague prior on difficulties

    delta ~ lognormal(0,1);  // weakly informative prior on discrimination

Constraining delta to be positive solves identifiability issue 3.

The other priors solve 1 and 2.

The relatively strong prior on abilities alpha coupled with
less data and the freedom to move the offset into beta,
drives the posterior of alpha to be standardized.  The relatively
weak prior on beta lets it float and absorb what would otherwise be
an intercept term (you can also fit the intercept hierarchically,
though this introduces yet another additive identifiability issue in
the hierarchical prior).

I prefer to make a full hierarchical model, but the above reproduces
a kind of baseline IRT that should fit close to what standard
maximum likelihood estimates fit.

- Bob

> Hi Bob,
>
> Thanks for your rapid and helpful response. To clarify, the IRT model I am running is more like an ideal-point model in
> that the responses are not coded as correct/incorrect but rather as yes/no.

And presumably the yeses and nos aren't all the same kind.

For instance, yea and nay votes don't line up with right or
left, because the bills may be right or left, so that
a nay vote may in one case be left and in others be right.
(This is assuming one dimensional models where the main
dimension you'll fit is party affiliation, at least in American congressional
politics.)

> Given that, I'm still not entirely clear on
> how best to identify the sign (the location and scale are identified via transformations on the difficulty and
> discrimination parameters).

These transforms may lead to their own issues if you're
not careful.

You can usually see the poorly identified parameters producing
low sample sizes --- at least I did in the IRT models I was
working on where the sign wasn't an issue.

> Would it work if I define the prior like this:
>
>      beta_raw ~ normal(0, 100);
>
> then fixed the sign of one item k like this:
>
>      beta[k] <- exp(beta_raw[k]);
>
> and finally applied the Jacobian adjustment you mentioned?:
>
>      lp__ <- lp__ + beta_raw[k];
>
> Forgive me for being slow to pick up what your saying---I do appreciate the help!

Yes, this corresponds to what Andrew and Jennifer suggest
in their book.  The easiest way to do it would be something like
this:

parameters {
    vector[K] beta_raw;
...
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[K] beta;
...
    beta <- beta_raw;
    beta[1] <- exp(beta[1]);
    lp__ <- lp__ + beta_raw[1];
...
}
model {
    beta ~ normal(0,10);
...
}

or whatever kind of prior you want to put on beta.

This has a somewhat odd interpretation in that you implicitly
are providing a half-normal prior on beta[1] (truncated to
0 to infinity) and a full normal prior on beta[2]...beta[K].
You don't need to divide by two in Stan, because you only need
the probability up to a proportion.

This only defines the sign, and if there's not enough data
for beta[1], I'd suspect it to not be very good at identifying.

In some cases, to determine location, you can pin down an actual
value.  Like fixing the ability or difficulty or discrimination
parameter of one student or item.  You can do this the same way by
setting beta[1] (or whatever) to a constant, and there's no need to
do any adjustment for that.

We should put more info about this in the manual.  It's just
that there are so many different kinds of models, we can't write
long treatises on each one, at least not in our doc.

- Bob

On 9/5/13 11:48 AM, Martin ï¿½mï¿½ra wrote:
> Oh, this is great. Thank you Bob for the effort.

I like nice problems like this --- it's more fun than
Sudoku :-)

> The results really match.

It is rather amazing that so many seemingly different
sampling algorithms get the same results.

> I have a few questions:
>    In my model, I was incrementing log posterior like this (see below). How does it actually differs from yours? It
> differs only in the one 1:m loop.
>

> *MY*
> /  for (i in 1:m) {/
> /    for (j in nmin:nmax) {/
> /      lp_for_n[j] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k[i], n[j], theta);/
> /    }/
> /    lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);/
>    }
> *YOURS*
> /  for (n in nmin:nmax)/
> /    lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- log(1.0 / ntot) + binomial_log(k,n,theta);/
> /}/
> /  lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(lp_for_n);/

It's just the order of the loops.  I found it easier to think about
computing the marginal for each n rather than looping the other way.
It also let me use vectorization.  The inner loop in my code could be
expanded to:

   lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- log(1.0 / ntot);

   for (i in 1:m)

      lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] <- lp_for_n[n - nmin + 1] + binomial_log(k[i],n,theta);

I also just used arithmetic rather than computing an n[j] to lookup.
Arithmetic's usually faster than memory lookup, and I find it easier
to understand.

>    How would you sample /n/ in qenerated quantities using theta? I couldn't solve it.

   generated quantities {
     int n;   // you could bound this, but I'm too lazy to go back and figure it out
     n <- categorical_rng(theta);
   }

This generates n from p(n|theta) = Categorical(n|theta).  You'll get one
random draw per iteration based on theta in that iteration, so that
p(theta,n|data) has the right joint distribution in the data, because
theta is generated from p(theta|data).

Note that you need to declare theta as a vector here --- it's the
only parameter categorical_rng accepts.

- Bob

Dear STAn users,

The following STAN code models a series system reliability where pass/fail data are collected at both components and system level. We specify a Negative log gamma (nlg) prior for eac

messages.body_plain:
The message indicates that NaN (not-a-number)
values into one of the binomials:

   > yc[j,i] ~ binomial(nt,Rc[j,i]); // component part

   > ys[j] ~ binomial(nt,Rs[j]); // system part

You have a lot of arithmetic in the model, some of which is
numerically unstable near boundaries (in the sense of
having possible underflows or overflows -- for instance, with
values less than -700 or so, exp underflows to 0).

Given their definitions:

 > for(i in 1:nc)
 > ...

 >   for(j in 1:N) {
 >     ytc[j,i]<- (t[j]/(t0[2]-t0[1]))*b[i]+ y0[i];
 >     Rc[j,i] <- inv_logit(ytc[j,i]);
 >   }

and

 > for(i in 1:N)
 >   Rs[i] <- prod(Rc[i]);

what's probably happening is that one or more of the ytc values are
infinite or NaN.  They can be NaN if the t0[2] - t0[1] values
are NaN, or if any of the other numbers are NaN.

So I'd try diagnosing by printing ytc and Rc values in
the code to see where they're going wrong, then maybe doing
the same for the inputs you think may not be right.

I'd also recomment using binomial_logit, where you don't
need to do the inverse logit transform --- it's more numerically
stable.

- Bob

On 9/5/13 5:13 PM, maxwell wrote:
> Dear STAn users,
>
> The following STAN code models a series system reliability where pass/fail data are collected at both components and
> system level. We specify a Negative log gamma (nlg) prior for each of the component prior. Clearly, that also implies a
> prior for the system reliability since R_syst = prod_i=1 to n R_compi. Note that if X ~ gamma(alpha, beta), then R =
> exp(-X) ~ NLG(alpha, beta). I hope that's enough as a background.
>
> Bcca_mod <- '
> data {
> real<lower=0> t0[2]; // time which the priors are specified

> int<lower=0> nt; // number of test at each time points
> real<lower=0> pi_m; // pi mixing proportion
> int yc[N,nc]; // component data -- component data by columns
> int ys[N]; // system data
> real<lower=0> t[N]; // time of data collection
> }

> real<lower=0> x0[nc];   // R(0) = exp(-xo) ## defines the negative log-gamma prior (NLG) prior
> real<lower=0> xdel[nc]; // Delta = exp(-del)
> }

> real yd[nc];
> real ytc[N,nc];

Hi Bob,
If you prefer to call it the real name... then the "banana" is fine with me :-)

I'm afraid my c++ is too weak even contemplate doing anything important like this! Feel free to do it - and ask any questions I could answer.  I'm not sure I follow you when you talk about turning it into a real test - perhaps you could elaborate please?

An alternate dataset is the "famous" NTDS published by Jelinski and Moranda in 1972 and heavily used in the discipline.... the published mode (by Goel and Okumoto 1979) is at the values alpha=33.99 and beta=0.00579 for the first 26 data points.

bugt <- c(9, 21, 32, 36, 43, 45, 50, 58, 63, 70, 71, 77,
  78, 87, 91, 92, 95, 98, 104, 105, 116, 149, 156, 247, 249, 250)
# restrict bugs to the first 26 elements to match the paper
# by Goel and Okumoto (1979)
N <- 26
bugs_dat <- list(N=N, bugs=bugt[1:N])

This looks less like a banana, and more like an L and requires about iter=120k and chains=4 to get n_eff approx 1000.

Currently working on Michael's plots...

cheers,
Seán

>    prob_n[n,] = exp(lp_for_n.samples[n,] - max_log_prob_n_propto[n]);
> }
> n = c()
>    for (i in 1:4000){
>      n[i]<-sample(27:500,1,prob=prob_n[i,],replace=T)
>
> But can you help me with implementing the sampling of n to Stan please? You said that I could use n
> <-categorical_rng(theta). But I don't get it. Theta is just scalar. On what bases it could be transformed to vector of n
> size? Did you mean to use lp_for_n instead? After transforming it first.

I'm not surprised I botched the normalization in R.  You shouldn't
need to sample, though --- you can just compute the distribution once you
have theta.  It looks just like what you did in R and then sampled.

And you do the same thing to sample in the generated quantities block
in Stan.  You need to define the prob_n vector as above and then use

    n <- categorical_rng(prob_n)

to sample.  For the categorical distribution, you'll need
to normalize, or you'll get a runtime error.

If you define prob_n as a transformed parameter, you can also use
it to define lp__ and it will also get printed.  Or you can define
it again in the generated quantities block as a local variable.

- Bob

* 914 respondents
* 12 choice tasks per respondent
* 4 alternatives per choice task
* 35 covariates per alternative
* 5 respondent covariates
* the process is using about 190MB of memory

messages.subject: Frozen periods on a simple model
messages.subject_clean: Frozen periods on a simple model
messages.body_plain:
One of Stan's selling points is the much faster mixing (per iteration) of the Markov chain, so I was surprised to find instead that I got very slow mixing on a simple model (see attached) due to the chain freezing for an extended period. The model is basically a logistic regression with some random effects. There are only two covariates. To get the ratio of MCSE to posterior SD down to 0.05 I found I had to go out to 2,560,000 iterations (with four chains). Half of those are adaptation, and the other half are sampling.

A plot of the lp__ samples from chain 4 reveals what is happening: the chain freezes for 50 * 1280 = 64,000 iterations, with nothing changing. Am I right that this means that the update was rejected 64,000 times in a row? What can cause that to happen? This is a simple model, after all.

In this example you only see one such frozen period, but I have seen other variations of this that had three out of the four chains having such frozen periods, one chain with three of them.

messages.body_plain:
This can happen when you have really bad tails -- the probability to transition out to that tail is very small, but by detailed balance that means that the probability of transitioning back is also really small.  In fact, the longer you run the more likely you are to jump to a tail and get stuck for long periods of time (ironically making your autocorrelations larger).  More sophisticated algorithms like RHMC can help, and using a variable step size can be enough to help you escape the tails, but the biggest improvement often comes from tightening up your prior distributions to make the tails more well-behaved.

messages.body_plain:
fmin and fmax if the inputs are continuous ("f" is
for floating point).  The reason we follow the C++
convention is to make it clear what the result type is:

   int max(int,int)
   int min(int,int)

   real fmax(real,real)
   real fmin(real,real)

Because int gets promoted to real, you can use fmax
and fmin with real or int inputs, but the outputs
are always real.

- Bob

On 9/7/13 7:00 PM, Martin ï¿½mï¿½ra wrote:
> Yes, I've tried using uniform prior for sigma1 (0,2) and sigma2 (0,50), but it doesn't help.
> Do you think LKJ parameterization would help? I'll try it tomorrow, seems complicated.

I don't think it'll help control the sampling.  But you'll
want to do something like this for higher dimensions than 2.

I reparameterized your model with a uniform prior for scale
instead of your vague inverse gamma for precision.

I also rewrote it to be a bit more efficient.   It may not be
ideal for pedagogical purposes ---  we struggle with the balance
between writing clear and writing fast models (ideally, Stan would be
smart enough to turn the former into the latter!).

It looks like the model mixes well and produces posterior draws for
r (correlation) that look like the values I see in figure 5.4.
And it's recovering reasonable mu values.  I'm not seeing the
wild multimodal posterior densities you plotted.

Where did your inputs come from and did they match the inputs
that generated fig 5.4 in the notes?  From the text,
it looks like

   sigmaerror = c(0.03,1)

was the input.  But in your code, it was

   sigmaerror = c(0.03,10).

Even if I use more error, I recover roughly the same values, though effective
sample size is quite a bit lower per iteration.

You also have this:

   mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(1000));

which is an informative prior on the scale you're at,
because the posterior mean of mu[2] is 98, whereas sqrt(1000)
is only 32, and there are only 12 noisy data points!

For instance, changing it to

   mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(10000));

raises the posterior mean estimate of mu[2] from 98 to 100.

This prior may also not be interacting well with the noise model that has
scale sd = 10 in the more extreme parameterization.

In general, it can be problematic when you're estimating values
near boundaries.  What happens in Stan is that we logit transform
bounded values (and then scale and translate them).  Values near
boundaries on (-1,1) represent logit values near -infinity or +infinity,
which can be difficult numerically.

Also, with the two different scales, Stan has to do more work.
Ideally, the data itself would be a bit more standardized.

> I'm actually doing it for EJ. I'm working on implementing all those models from the book.

:-)  Small world, of course.

- Bob

P.S.  I see you have kappa coefficients coming up next.  I'd suggest
       looking at something like Dawid and Skene's 1979 measurement error
       model for data annotation in addition to kappa.

Vector transpose  -- it turns a row vector, which is
what y[i] picks out, to a column vector (or just "vector"),
which is what multi_normal expects.

> And is it better to use col(x,j)
> instead of having array of vectors? I thought that in manual the second option was prefered.

So yes, if you made y an array of vectors, that'd be faster than
using y[i]'.

> I've also tried mu ~ normal(0,sqrt(10000)), but it's resulting in similar correlation posterior.
>
> Can I actually build on results from Jags and BUGS? Or they can be wrong in this case?

Unfortunately, all these methods can fall over in the same situations,
which typically involve highly variable scales in the posterior.  What happens
is that there are sharp transitions in log posterior (for instance, when a hierarchical
variance parameter goes to zero), which are hard for all of these methods to
deal with.  RMHMC will be better, but it can be slow per iteration and
limited in scalability.

I'm worried about the two versions of this model being different in Stan.  If
everything else agreed other than my model, my model might be wrong.  Seems
more likely than all the other ones being wrong.

- Bob

> Can I ignore the warning about matrix being positive definite?

Yes, the problem arises during the simulation of the
position of the parameters under Hamiltonian dynamics.
We need to trade off the time granularity of the simulation
(step size) vs. number of steps.  With smaller step size,
we get more accurate transition approximations, but it
takes more steps.  This balance is tuned for optimal
sampling during warmup.  The resulting balance occassionally
rejects because of too-large steps using only gradient
taking you outside of support for constrained variables
like covariance matrices.

> Or is it better to give bounds to r (-0.9999,0.9999)?

That will probably do it, but whether it's better or not is a matter
of where you think the results will be.  If you get estimates near the
boundary, then you want wider bounds (closer to 0 and 1).   The other
alternative is to use a stronger prior pushign values to 0.
That's why we like the LKJ priors --- you can set up a correlation matrix
that favors the identity with an adjustable strength, then use a scale
vector (i.e., the sd of the dimensions) to convert it to a correlation
matrix.  So you independently control amount of shrinkage toward
identity correlation and the scales of the dimensions.

> Thanks for your time Bob.

You're welcome.  The examples you've brought up have been fun and
we want to make sure Stan is usable in as many situations and for
as many kinds of models as possible.

Speaking of which, do you have plans to distribute the models when
you're done coding them?  Or do a comparison with JAGS/BUGS?  That'd
be fantastic, I think, for us and the BUGS and JAGS developers.
What we're interested in is for efficiency and scalability are:

   (a) speed to convergence, especially from diffuse
       initializations,

   (b) mixing speed after convergence in terms of number
       of effective samples per second, and

   (c) memory use.

We're interested not only in averages, but also variation, though I'm
not so sure how to measure that other than histograms of the measurements
above.  We've been finding that our chains can be pretty variable in how long they take.

- Bob

messages.subject: Growth Mixture Model implemented in Stan
messages.subject_clean: Growth Mixture Model implemented in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

I would like to know if anyone has implemented a Growth Mixture Model
(GMM) in Stan ? More generally I would like to know the experts opinions
on the suitability of Stan for estimating GMMs

To avoid confusion, here I consider a GMM to be an extension of a Latent
Growth Curve model (LGCM) in the following sense. In LGCM, repeated
measures of some variable are modelled as a function of a small number
of latent variables, for example an intercept and slope. Such a model
can also be considered as a mixed effects / multilevel model where the
random effects (random intercepts and random slopes in this case)
correspond to the latent growth variables.

GMM can then be viewed as an extension of LGCM which allows for
differences in latent growth variables across unobserved subpopulations,
modelled as latent classes.

Individuals are classified by estimating their posterior probabilities
of class membership. The number of latent classes is generally specified
in advance - models with different numbers of classes are compared using
statistics such as BIC (as well as expert a priori considerations) to
determine the optimum number of classes.

Covariates may enter the model as predictors of the latent growth
variables, and/or as predictors of the latent class variable.

In more complex models, the latent class variable may also predict a
distal outcome variable.

The variance-covariance matrix of the latent growth variables is often
an area of modelling focus.

The variance-covariance matrix of the measurement-level residual
variances is also an area of modelling focus - for example they are
sometimes all constrained to be equal, sometimes freely estimated, and
sometimes assumed to be autoregressive.

Convergence is often a problem with these kinds of finite mixture
models. The variance of the latent growth variables is sometimes
constrained to zero in order to achieve convergence. MPlus is often
used, using maximum likelihood (EM algorithm) with thousands of
different random starting values to overcome the problem of local
solutions.

I wondered whether a fully Bayesian approach in Stan with
suitable/flexible choices of priors would be a good alternative ?

In a nutshell - is Stan a good choice for fitting these kinds of models
? Has anyone has any success ? If so I would love to hear about the
results, particularly compared to using Mplus.

Thanks
RL

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Growth Mixture Model implemented in Stan
messages.body_plain:
You probably want to take a look at the mixture modeling
chapter in the Stan manual -- it's a bit tricky how to do it.
No problem in theory as long as there are preset numbers of
classes (or you can approximate unbounded with a big fixed number).

Stan's set up to let you change priors easily, so moving
from independent to time series is no big deal.  It can have
a big impact on sampling, so parameterization and efficiency
become important considerations.

As to particular priors, that's going to depend on your data
and how much of it there is.  The less data there is, the
more careful you have to be with priors to control computation
(and control the posterior for inference).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I don't think it's a bug --- I just think this
is a very hard model to fit for three reasons:

1.  You have improper priors on mu and sigma, which
gives the posterior a lot of latitude in these parameters.

2.  Given mu, there's not much constraint on sigma because
of the truncation.  As sigma gets larger, the distribution
just gets flatter, but it starts out pretty flat, which
is related to 3.

3.  You don't have much data given that you're constraining
centered at +/- 1 sd, which gives you a relatively flat
distribution.

I constrained sigma to the interval (0,10) but left
the improper prior on mu, and it fits fine with 2000
rnorm generations (about 1400 actual data points).

If you only provide 1000 draws from rnorm (700 data points),
the traceplot has a lot of outliers for mu (and hence for sigma, which
follows it).  You could potentially run many more iterations,
because the posterior mode looks right in the traceplots.
With 10K iterations/chain, you start to see the right value
for mu, but the posterior's still very broad for sigma.

You can try to control the problem with better priors on
sigma or mu or more data.  But otherwise, I think Stan's doing
the right thing.

- Bob

R code
===================================
library('rstan');

set.seed(1234)
mu <- 1;
sigma <- 2;
y <- rnorm(2000, 1, 2);

L <- -1
U <- 3
y <- y[y >= L & y <= U]
N <- length(y)

fit <- stan("sp_rm_trunc.stan", data=c("N","L","U","y"),
             seed=123456);

print(fit);

Model
==================================

data {
   int<lower=0> N;
   real L;
   real U;
   vector<lower=L, upper=U>[N] y;
}
parameters {
   real mu;

   real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma;

}
model {
   for (n in 1:N)
     y[n] ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[L, U];
}

accuracies and biases --- so it's also related to education
models like IRT if you start thinking about things like
item difficulty.

Yes, it's the usual the cumulative distribution function
for the distribution.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function

We need to write that out more clearly in the manual.  I'll
put it on the to-do list.  The functional forms need to go in, too,
but they're very hairy, so we haven't gotten around to it yet.

We're adding cdf() and ccdf() in Stan 2 on the log scales (ccdf() is
1 - cdf()).  And we'll be putting in ongoing work to make them more efficient
and more arithmetically stable.

> binomial_cdf(x, size, p) = pbinon(x, size, p) = P[X <= x]
>
> and P[15 <= X <= 25] = P[X <= 25] - P[X < 15] = P[X <= 25] - P[X <= 14].

You can always try this stuff in Stan, too, using the generated
quantities block (or transformed parameters, though generated
quantities are more efficient).

> In R:
>
>  > p <- 0
>  > for (i in 15:25) p <- p + choose(50,i) * 0.4^i * (1-0.4)^(50-i)
>  > p
> [1] 0.8887012
>  > pbinom(25, 50, 0.4) - pbinom(14, 50, 0.4)
> [1] 0.8887012

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Summary: While estimating a model memory use increased steadily,
resulting in a dead job or unresponsive system around 8G.  Anything I
can do about that?

I ran a model for 200 iterations and 1 chain; it finished in about 65
seconds.
  > system.time(r <- stan(model_code = stan_model, data=stanDat,
  +                       iter=200, chains=1))

Then I used the model compiled at the previous step to do something more:
system.time(r2 <- stan(fit=r, data=stanDat, iter=2000, chains=3))

That ran for a few minutes and then I got "Process R killed".

I rebuilt with debugging level non-optimization, as suggested in the
FAQ. The job took steadily increasing amounts of memory.  I killed it
when it was just over 8G and my system became unresponsive.

Is this typical, or is something wrong with my model or the underlying
code (like a memory leak)?  The problem doesn't seem that big: 15
parameters, ~2,500 observations with 3 variables for each. It's a
multinomial model.  I added value to the comments.

I'm using rstan from git as of this morning.  The model is
data {
    int<lower=0> N; // number of partners ~2,500
    int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race 5
        // K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
    int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates 3
    int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N];  // partner race
    //int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of respondents
    matrix[N, J] x;  // covariates
}
parameters {
     matrix[J, K] beta;
}
model {
     vector[K] beta_x;
      for(ir in 1:J)
        beta[ir] ~ normal(0, 5);
     for(n in 1:N) {
       beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)';
       pEthnic[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta_x));
     }
}

The model has a number of oddities, at least when viewed from my
frequentist experience:
1. no intercept
2. overdetermined outcomes.  The outcome is one of 5 categories; all 5
are modeled.
3. overdetermined covariates.  Each observation is one of 3 categories;
each category has a dummy variable.
Other example models I looked at seemed similarly over-determined, so I
thought maybe this was OK (though the example I copied from did have an
intercept).

I based this on the "Speeding Up Multinomial Logistic Regressions in
Stan" thread started April 19.  I tried to follow Bob's advice about
using vector and matrix arithmetic when possible, but my efforts to
imitate the code revisions he gave were not successful.  The manual
suggests (x[n] * beta)' is not the most efficient way to go.  (I skipped
the stuff about beta_raw to simplify).

Any tips or advice would be great.

Running under R 2.15.1, Debian wheezy amd64 bit.  This is without any of
my efforts to use system boost or eigen headers.  I refreshed rstan (and
the stan subproject) and built the tarball from the upper level
makefile.  Then I did an R CMD INSTALL on that tarball, using a local
path for installation.

Ross Boylan

P.S.  Time for the initial 200 iterations with 65 seconds with
optimization, 763 seconds without optimization.  Wow!

messages.body_plain:
Hello Bob

On Monday, September 9, 2013 8:07:05 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 9/9/13 6:43 PM, Jason Morgan wrote:
> > Dear Bob,
> >
> > On Sunday, September 8, 2013 8:37:15 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >
> >
> >     It's efficient.  I wish it were more elegant, but I don't know
> >     a better way to do it.
> >
> >
> > Thanks. Glad I was on the right track, despite the inelegance.
> >
> >     If you constrain parameters to intervals as you did, you should make
> >
> >     sure they're wide enough to cover any reasonable posterior value.
> >     At that point, you have a proper uniform distribution on the parameters,
> >     so you don't need to add normal priors unless you believe their
> >     shape is reasonable (that is, that those [0,5] constrained params
> >     are more likely to be 2.5 than other values).
> >
> >
> > For actual data, I will have to play with the prior (and will start with a uniform). For my simulations, I wanted
> > something that would estimate quickly. Is there a clear way to tell if the constraints aren't wide enough?
>
> Yes --- you'll see samples getting drawn from very close to the
> boundaries.

That makes sense.

> >
> >     What non-identifiabilities do you have?  It looks from the
> >     model that it's just an offset identity due to this line:
> >
> >       >              D[idx] <- sqrt(dot_self(pos[i] - pos[j]));
> >
> >     So you probably have to pin down values for pos[] more than you have.
> >     You can fix one value to a hard constraint.
> >
> >     Or you can add in an intercept and give pos stronger centering priors.
> >
> >     How do you choose the value(s) to fix?
> >
> >
> > The response is a function of the pairwise distances (the D vectorin the model), which are invariant to translation,
> > rotation, and reflection, but the latent positions are not. In my substantive applications, I have a good idea about
> > where some of the observations should be placed in the latent space; e.g., I know (or can argue) that particular
> > politicians are to the right or left of others. I could simply fix the positions of a couple actors, but in some of my
> > applications I would like to allow a little more flexibility,
>
> You can constrain signs and leave their positions undetermined.  Or you can
> do what Andrew suggests and take a very right (or left) politician and use
> them as the basis, fixing just their position.

For some of the Senate data I was analyzing, I was fixing the positions of two Senators, which worked well. But in the contexts I am more interested in (Eastern European parliaments), things are somewhat less structured. I was hoping to let things to "float" a bit more freely -- especially since I am extending the model to dynamic data and the number of fixed parameters was starting to climb and since there isn't a large body of established data on politicians' relative positions to draw upon. I do think constraining signs may work well, since I can make a plausible case for the positions of particular politicians. I'm just trying to get this model as well thought out as possible since my real dataset is quite large.

> > since the positions are more debatable (this is something
> > of a "cosmetic issue", since the relative distances shouldn't be affected). Of course, in testing the model, setting
> > particular observations is arbitrary -- I'm just doing it to make sure the model is doing what I think it should.
> >
> > Another option I have thought about is just to deal with the non-invariance of the latent positions through
> > post-processing; i.e., some form of multidimensional scaling.
>
> This is problematic for Stan's adaptation, because it's
> trying to adapt to scales during warmup that aren't identified.

That's what I suspected.

> > This is what HRHdo in the original paper -- they perform
> > a Procrustes transformation with the pairwise geodesic distances as the reference distance matrix.
>
> No idea what this means, but I'm assuming Procrustes is a
> reference to the bed.

That's where they get the term, though it's a bit of a misnomer -- the procedure makes one set of positions as close as possible to another, reference set, while remaining shape-preserving. No legs are lopped off.

> Andrew also worked through this option and even has code
> in his and Jennifer's book.  But it's not a great idea for
> Stan.

I will take a closer look, even though it may not be a great option here.

> > This appears to work
> > for their applications but seems to me to be a bit ad hoc and may not translate well to a broader set of problems where
> > the latent positions are substantively meaningful. I could also just do the MDS by using particular observations as a
> > reference, but that doesn't get around the issue of having to pick fixed locations for those observations.
>
> If there's a translation non-identifiability, this shouldn't
> be a big deal.
>
> > Another
> > reason to have the observations constrained in the model, as I currently do, is that it allows me to run and compare
> > multiple chains.
>
> Absolutely.  You can also do the transforms in a generated quantities
> block, which lets you do the same thing in Stan.  But again, it's
> better to have the parameters in the model itself identified if possible.

I played with generated quantities some, but for my larger datasets, I was concerned with the size of the saved objects. Getting the parameters identified seems to me to be the best bet at this point.

> I'd be very interested to see what happens with a post-transform.
> And we're always happy to help with concrete fitting issues when
> you get a candidate model defined.

Thanks. I appreciate it. I have played with some test (fake) datasets over the last couple days, and the model seems to be working pretty well. I am now going to start working on fitting the model to the data in the original paper and then move on to the dynamic model, which is my ultimate objective.

> > Sorry, that's probably more info that you wanted, but it's my current thinking on the issue.
>
> I always find more easier to understand than less.  I find I often
> answer my own questions when trying to write them out in long form.
> - Bob

Thanks again.

~Jason

On 9/12/13 8:34 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> Summary: While estimating a model memory use increased steadily, resulting in a dead job or unresponsive system around
> 8G.  Anything I can do about that?

Running from the command line, models should allocate
memory before the first iteration and never need more
memory than the amount used after the first iteration.
If it's going up otherwise, it may be a signal of a memory
leak.

Your parameter is a J x K matrix and you'll need enough memory in
R to store the number of samples times a J x K matrix times 8 bytes.
At minimum (not accounting for R overhead), this will require

    2000     iterations/chain
    * 3      chains
    * 8      bytes/double
    * 1      double/parameter
    * J * K  parameters/iteration

=  2000 * 3 * 8 * J * K bytes

If that's a lot less than 8 GB, it may be the sign of a problem.

> I ran a model for 200 iterations and 1 chain; it finished in about 65 seconds.
>   > system.time(r <- stan(model_code = stan_model, data=stanDat,
>   +                       iter=200, chains=1))

Can you do that for 4 chains and if so, does it produce enough
effective samples?  If so, you may not need to run longer.

If the memory's too big or there's too much correlation in the
samples, you can thin the output, which should cut down on memory
usage.

> Then I used the model compiled at the previous step to do something more:
> system.time(r2 <- stan(fit=r, data=stanDat, iter=2000, chains=3))
>
> That ran for a few minutes and then I got "Process R killed".
>
> I rebuilt with debugging level non-optimization, as suggested in the FAQ. The job took steadily increasing amounts of
> memory.  I killed it when it was just over 8G and my system became unresponsive.

I have no idea what this does w.r.t. R, but just at the C++
level, the optimization level shouldn't have only a minimal impact on
memory usage.

> Is this typical, or is something wrong with my model or the underlying code (like a memory leak)?  The problem doesn't
> seem that big: 15 parameters, ~2,500 observations with 3 variables for each. It's a multinomial model.  I added value to
> the comments.
>
> I'm using rstan from git as of this morning.

Very brave of you!  We're trying to keep the development branches
of RStan and Stan in working order.

> The model is
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of partners ~2,500
>     int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race 5
>         // K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
>     int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates 3
>     int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N];  // partner race
>     //int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of respondents
>     matrix[N, J] x;  // covariates
> }
> parameters {
>      matrix[J, K] beta;
> }
> model {
>      vector[K] beta_x;
>       for(ir in 1:J)
>         beta[ir] ~ normal(0, 5);

Replace this loop with the vectorized form:

   beta ~ normal(0,5);

Is 5 a reasonable prior scale here in that you expect
the posterior for beta to be in the [-10,10] range or so?

>      for(n in 1:N) {
>        beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)';
>        pEthnic[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta_x));
>      }
> }

Stan 2 (the current dev branch), will let you do this:

    pEthnic[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta_x);

It should be a bit more efficient than categorical(softmax(beta_x)).

It'll also be more efficient if the covariate type is:

    row_vector[J] x[N];  // covariates

Then there's no memory allocation for x[n].

> The model has a number of oddities, at least when viewed from my frequentist experience:
> 1. no intercept
> 2. overdetermined outcomes.  The outcome is one of 5 categories; all 5 are modeled.
> 3. overdetermined covariates.  Each observation is one of 3 categories; each category has a dummy variable.
> Other example models I looked at seemed similarly over-determined, so I thought maybe this was OK (though the example I
> copied from did have an intercept).

None of this should matter for memory usage.

> I based this on the "Speeding Up Multinomial Logistic Regressions in Stan" thread started April 19.  I tried to follow

>
> Ross Boylan
>
> P.S.  Time for the initial 200 iterations with 65 seconds with optimization, 763 seconds without optimization.  Wow!

try to build code that would be efficient if it wasn't
compiled with optimization.

Dear Bob,

I just had an appointment with someone from our Biostatistics department to help me with the change in variables. However, we still got stuck and were hoping that you could explain your suggestion for a very simple example (attached below)?

Thank you very much,
Marcel

parameters{
  simplex[4] phi[2];
}

transformed parameters{
 vector[2] logit_r1;
 logit_r1[1] <- logit( phi[1,3] + phi[1,4] );
 logit_r1[2] <- logit( phi[2,3] + phi[2,4] );
}

model{
 phi[1] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
 phi[2] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
 logit_r1 ~ multi_normal_prec( [..] , [..,..] );
 // account for change in variables
 lp__ <- lp__ + ..
}

> Date: Sat, 31 Aug 2013 17:22:14 -0400
> From: ca...@alias-i.com
> To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
> Subject: Re: [stan-users] Change of variables

>
> If y are the unconstrained values and x = f(y) are
> the constrained values, then if you write
>
> x ~ foo(theta);
>
> you need to add the log of the absolute determinant of
> the Jacobian matrix for the transform f. The entries
> J[m,n] in the Jacobian are:
>
> J[m,n] = d/d.y[m] { f(y)[n] }
>
> I don't understand the intent of what you're doing, but you
> have two priors on the matrix, one from the sampling statement on
> logit_r1 and one from the sampling statement on phi.
>
> If you just put the priors on phi, you can transform and use
> the result as a parameter w/o a Jacobian adjustment. If you drop
> the priors on phi and go with a prior on logit_r1, then you'll need
> the Jacobian of the transform. If you leave them both, it's essentially
> a product prior.
>
> a ~ foo(theta);
> a ~ bar(rho);
>
> means
>
> p(a) propto foo(a|theta) * bar(a|rho);
>
> It doesn't look like the derivatives are too bad, but
> all the indexing looks like it's going to be fiddly unless
> you can reexpress in terms of simpler vectors.
>
> - Bob
>
>

> >
> > I have a mathematical question (so perhaps not suited for the list) but I'm sufficiently stuck to give it a try. I want

messages.body_plain:
There's a small problem with truncating real values to
integers --- you lose any autodiff information.  So if
the truncation's part of the model, it may not work as you
intend.

Also, as an efficiency note, ifelse() evaluates both of
its arguments, which isn't a big deal in this case because
c is a plain vector.  On the other hand, an if { } else { }
conditional statement only evaluates the block for the
condition that goes through.

- Bob

> of particular politicians. I'm just trying to get this model as well thought out as possible since my real dataset is

again.

If the offset really isn't identified, there's not much you can
do about it other than stronger priors and an intercept, or fixing
some of the values.  At least that I can think of.

>

>

>     Absolutely.  You can also do the transforms in a generated quantities
>     block, which lets you do the same thing in Stan.  But again, it's
>     better to have the parameters in the model itself identified if possible.
>
>
> I played with generated quantities some, but for my larger datasets, I was concerned with the size of the saved objects.
> Getting the parameters identified seems to me to be the best bet at this point.

That is a concern.  Stan and it's I/O are pretty fast,
but it slows down R's uptake.

>     I'd be very interested to see what happens with a post-transform.
>     And we're always happy to help with concrete fitting issues when
>     you get a candidate model defined.
>
> Thanks. I appreciate it. I have played with some test (fake) datasets over the last couple days, and the model seems to
> be working pretty well. I am now going to start working on fitting the model to the data in the original paper and then
> move on to the dynamic model, which is my ultimate objective.

Excellent plan!  We're proponents of validating with fake
data sets then moving up the complexity of the model.

messages.subject: subscripts/documentation
messages.subject_clean: subscripts/documentation
messages.body_plain:
There are some points at which the documentation on subscripts and
arrays/matrices/vectors is unclear or, possibly, incorrect.  This is
with  the 1.3.0 pdf "Stan Modeling Language" dated 12 April, 2013.

1.
p. 152 has
e <- d[1]
e is an array with leading dimension 4 while d, after dropping the first
dimension, has leading dimension 3.  I don't think they are
conformable.

Also
x <- d[4, 3, 5, 2]
x <- e[3, 5, 2]
are said to be the same, but I think the second line is equivalent to
d[1, 3, 5, 2] and so they are different.
Have I misunderstood?

2.
P. 166 says "see Section ?? for a full explanation" about 1/4 of the way
down the page.

3.
The documentation seems to be silent on mixing arrays and vectors or
matrices such as
real a[3, 4];
matrix[3, 4] b;
row_vector[4] r;
b <- a;
b+a;
r <- a[2];

I would take that as a sign that such operations are illegal, and I
think I've seen error messages when I inadvertently tried those
operations.

It would be helpful to be explicit.

Also, it's confusing to have two ways of doing about the same thing
(with apologies to Perl)--but that's a more complicated design issue.

4.
The discussion of the dump format in  chapter 6 does not technically
discuss matrices, vectors, row vectors, or arrays of those types.  I did
not realize this on first reading because I did not appreciate that
array was a distinct type from those other subscriptable entities.

I think the only reasonable reading it that section 6.3 covers all
subscriptable types, with the order of subscripts being consistent with
the ordering given in other sections, namely that the array indices come
first in mixed types and the ordering assumes the subscripts vary most
rapidly from left to right ("last column major order" in some parts of
the docs).  But it might be good to be explicit.

5.
The discussion of partial subscripting in 20.4, 20.5 and 21.5 provides
no indication that such expressions can be assigned to.  Though 22.1
explains that such assignments are valid, some indication of that in the
initial presentation of partial subscripting seems natural to me.

Ross Boylan

On 9/13/13 9:01 AM, M.F. Jonker wrote:
> Dear Bob,
>
> I just had an appointment with someone from our Biostatistics department to help me with the change in variables.
> However, we still got stuck and were hoping that you could explain your suggestion for a very simple example (attached
> below)?
>
> Thank you very much,
> Marcel
>
>
> parameters{
>    simplex[4] phi[2];
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>   vector[2] logit_r1;
>   logit_r1[1] <- logit( phi[1,3] + phi[1,4] );
>   logit_r1[2] <- logit( phi[2,3] + phi[2,4] );
> }
>
> model{
>   phi[1] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
>   phi[2] ~ dirichlet( [....] );
>   logit_r1 ~ multi_normal_prec( [..] , [..,..] );
>   // account for change in variables
>   lp__ <- lp__ + ..
> }

Why do you want to parameterize like this?  It seems
like it's asking for non-identifiability.  Or is there
something else going on with the phi?

The way you have it parameterized, you actually put
priors on phi twice, once through phi itself and once
in the transformed form with logit_r1 ~.  Is that
really what you intended?    It might be if the arguments
to multi_norm_prec are reversed, because

    y ~ multi_normal_prec(mu,Omega)

does the same thing as

    mu ~ multi_normal_prec(y,Omega);

So what's the first arg to multi_normal_prec?

I'm really bad at this myself.  Ben's always helped me out.
Hopefully he'll chime in here.

Technically, you need to calculate the determinant of
the Jacobian of the multivariate transform.  Where I always
get stuck is figuring out what the transform dimensions are.
And it tends to work out that the determinant is easy because
the the Jacobian is diagonal or lower triangular.

- Bob

>
>
>
>  > Date: Sat, 31 Aug 2013 17:22:14 -0400
>  > From: ca...@alias-i.com
>  > To: stan-...@googlegroups.com

>  > If y are the unconstrained values and x = f(y) are
>  > the constrained values, then if you write

>  > x ~ foo(theta);
>  >
>  > you need to add the log of the absolute determinant of
>  > the Jacobian matrix for the transform f. The entries
>  > J[m,n] in the Jacobian are:
>  >
>  > J[m,n] = d/d.y[m] { f(y)[n] }
>  >
>  > I don't understand the intent of what you're doing, but you
>  > have two priors on the matrix, one from the sampling statement on
>  > logit_r1 and one from the sampling statement on phi.
>  >
>  > If you just put the priors on phi, you can transform and use
>  > the result as a parameter w/o a Jacobian adjustment. If you drop
>  > the priors on phi and go with a prior on logit_r1, then you'll need
>  > the Jacobian of the transform. If you leave them both, it's essentially
>  > a product prior.
>  >
>  > a ~ foo(theta);
>  > a ~ bar(rho);
>  >
>  > means
>  >
>  > p(a) propto foo(a|theta) * bar(a|rho);
>  >
>  > It doesn't look like the derivatives are too bad, but
>  > all the indexing looks like it's going to be fiddly unless
>  > you can reexpress in terms of simpler vectors.
>  >
>  > - Bob

On 9/13/13 1:54 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:

> If I do 200 iterations and throw away the first 100, does (Sampling)
> refer to the last 100, or to all 200?

I'm not sure what context you're asking about, but when
the message changes from adapting to sampling, it means
you're past warmup.  So the default in running 200 iterations
is to use the first 100 for warmup and keep the last 200
for inference.

For many problems, Stan converges much faster than that, but
it's a good default because it's at most going to cost you
a factor of two in time.  If you need a gazillion samples,
it makes sense to set the warmup period lower.

> I later did multiple chains in one run; it looked as stan repeats the
> tuning with each chain.  Is that how it operates?

Yes.

> Is  that desirable?

Maybe.  The motivation is partly practical.  If we do this all
independently, we don't need any inter-chain communication, so it's
easy to parallelize chains.  Another motivation is to diagnose
convergence problems that might not otherwise arise if you only
run a single adaptation.  Often, at least in Stan 1.3 (hopefully a
bit less in Stan 2.0), a single chain will get stuck because of
adaptation failing.  (We can also get stuck by transitioning to
low probability areas and having a tough time transitioning back ---
detailed balance is a tough law to respect :-))

Having said that, we are thinking about ways to do inter-chain
communication on adaptation.

Any suggestions anybody might have on how to do this would be
appreciated.

- Bob

simpler for users) approach: doing an initial run (phases 1 and maybe 2

> Since stan's default was 2,000 iterations, I figured 200 was grossly
> inadequate, and probably not even sufficient for convergence.

We based that on JAGS, but then Stan tends to converge faster and
mix better, so we're cranking the default number of iterations down
to 100.  It should probably be 20 --- just enough to get the model
adapting a little and sampling a little to make sure there are no
big problems in the model itself.

It's problem specific as to how fast convergence is and then what
the mixing rate is, and then application specific as to how many effective
samples you need.

> I guess the main thing to do is watch Rhat and effective sample sizes.
> For the more complicated model with clustering I just did 6 parallel
> runs with 500 iterations each.  The Rhats look as if they are almost all
> 1.0--suggesting I might get away with a shorter burn-in?--and n_eff is
> around 100 for my key parameters, often much higher for the cluster
> effects, but only 29 for sigma and 27 for lp__.  The latter 2 have rhat
> of 1.2.

Look at the traceplots in R.  The warmup (what was previously called "burnin")
is the greyed over first part.  You can usually eyeball about how many
iterations convergence takes --- then pad it a bit (say a factor of 2)
to be safe for future runs.

> Are the values for lp__ important?  That is, if sigma had worked out
> better but lp__ still had the low effective size and elevated Rhat,
> would that be a sign that more iterations were in order?

Not really, because lp__ isn't something we're using for inference.
It's the unnormalized log probability of the model.  You do want to
look at it across runs to compare how well the model fits.  You do want
it to mix, but it doesn't need a high effective sample size unless you're
doing inference on it.

> I guess the values for sigma and lp_ indicate I need more iterations and
> more burn-in.  Is that a reasonable inference?

What do you need the output for?  If you're just trying to estimate
posterior means, we report MCMC error --- that's the accuracy of
the mean estimate.  If you need tail estimates for probabilities, you
need many more samples.

Usually when MCMC error is an order of magnitude less than the quantity
being estimated you're in pretty good shape using the samples for inference.

> The model parameters are of secondary interest for my current project
> which is to assess "causal" effects within a system for which the model
> is one equation.

The goal's always the same --- look at what you're trying to compute and
see how much that varies.

> As you may recall, I've also been working on imputation.  I speculate
> that is the setting in which the standards for "good enough" estimates
> are loosest.

Same deal, but I can see why this wouldn't require tight estimates.

- Bob

> On Fri, 2013-09-13 at 14:07 -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> On 9/13/13 1:54 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>>> If I do 200 iterations and throw away the first 100, does (Sampling)
>>> refer to the last 100, or to all 200?
>>
>> I'm not sure what context you're asking about,
> The run I just did.
>>   but when
>> the message changes from adapting to sampling, it means
>> you're past warmup.  So the default in running 200 iterations
>> is to use the first 100 for warmup and keep the last 200
>> for inference.
>
> I thought there were 3 phases
> 1) tune algorithmic parameters (if not pre-specified)
> 2) run chain to get it to the "long-run" state, tossing results
> 3) run chain to get target distribution, keeping results.
>
> Do 1 + 2 happen at the same time?  Does "warmup" = 2 or 1+2.

"Warmup" is just Andrew's new coinage for "burnin".  It's a better
physical analogy, but is confusing our users.  The new edition of
BDA no longer mentions "burnin".

Warmup = 1 + 2.  This is just like in JAGS and BUGS, which also
do adaptation during "burnin".

In RStan, we keep the warmup "samples" too, so you can diagnose
how quickly we converge to the high mass part of the posterior.

>>
>> For many problems, Stan converges much faster than that, but
>> it's a good default because it's at most going to cost you
>> a factor of two in time.  If you need a gazillion samples,
>> it makes sense to set the warmup period lower.
>>
>>> I later did multiple chains in one run; it looked as stan repeats the
>>> tuning with each chain.  Is that how it operates?
>>
>> Yes.
>>
>>> Is  that desirable?
>>
>> Maybe.  The motivation is partly practical.  If we do this all
>> independently, we don't need any inter-chain communication, so it's
>> easy to parallelize chains.  Another motivation is to diagnose
>> convergence problems that might not otherwise arise if you only
>> run a single adaptation.  Often, at least in Stan 1.3 (hopefully a
>> bit less in Stan 2.0), a single chain will get stuck because of
>> adaptation failing.  (We can also get stuck by transitioning to
>> low probability areas and having a tough time transitioning back ---
>> detailed balance is a tough law to respect :-))
>>
>> Having said that, we are thinking about ways to do inter-chain
>> communication on adaptation.
>>
>> Any suggestions anybody might have on how to do this would be
>> appreciated.
>
> I was thinking of a simpler to implement (for stan developers, maybe not
> simpler for users) approach: doing an initial run (phases 1 and maybe 2
> in my list above) on one machine, and then parallelize step 3 with every
> parallel process getting the results of the initial run.  In particular,
> model compilation and tuning would happen only once.

One issue is that Andrew's very keen to start at diffuse starting points.

This interacts badly with adaptation.  The problem we're facing with
adaptation is that the settings that let you move from a far-away initial
point to something more typical are different than the settings you want to
use once you've gotten to the high-mass part of the posterior.

The other issue is that if we only run a single chain, then say, randomize
around where it left off, we won't have as good a diagnostic on poor
mixing (my interpretation of what Andrew keeps saying).

> In this model the only inter-chain communication is  from the master to
> the slave at the start and and from the slave to the master at the end,
> i.e., same pattern as now.

Right.

> Whether that would be a good idea depends partly on how safe it is to
> tune once.

My understanding is not very --- see above.

What we're likely to do, since tuning is global, is to run multiple
chains then make sure they converge to the same tuning parameters, and
somehow allow them to share info across chains.

- Bob

I'm responding to too many people, so I'm losing track of
their contexts.  Digits can be controlled in bin/print
in the GitHub version of Stan.  Digits can be controlled
in the usual way in R using digits=5, etc., in the print
statement, e.g., print(stan.fit, digits=5).

Loosening priors can indeed lead to lower R-hat values and
wider posterior intervals.

Which terms are hard to estimate totally depend on the problem.
In some cases, models are only weakly identified, meaning
it takes a lot of samples before the posterior means start to
look right.  In linear regressions, sigma is usually dead easy
to fit.

Research software's usually slow because not enough people are working
on it in a directed enough way.  We're bogged down because
we're trying to do too many things at once.

messages.subject: Imputing missing sample sizes for a binomial density in STAN?
messages.subject_clean: Imputing missing sample sizes for a binomial density in STAN?
messages.body_plain:
I am wondering if it is possible to impute missing sample sizes (integers) for use in binomial densities in STAN.

To explain the issue:
Lets assume we want to know how the prevalence of a disease varies as a function of distance to the nearest urban center.

Say for instance we have a population living on a reserve and from census data we know that there are 6,000 individuals living in the reserve, distributed across 50 villages. Further, we know from anthropological studies the village-level population of 40 of these villages (say 4,000 people in total). Thus, we know that 2,000 individuals are distributed across the remaining 10 villages, but we don't know the exact population per village. Finally, we have count data on the number of cases of infections per village reported by the municipal hospital, and data on the distance between each village and the nearest urban center.

Ideally, were would like a model like:

number.infected ~ binomial( Population, inv_logit(Theta) )

where Theta is modeled as a function of distance to the nearest urban center.

This raises some issues in STAN, however, since we need Population to take only integer values, but we have to impute missing population sizes

What seems plausible is using a Dirichlet distribution of length 10, to estimate how the remaining 2,000 people should be allocated across the remaining 10 districts. This vector could serve as a prior for a multinomial distribution of size N=2,000, which would transform the unit simplex into a vector of integers that exactly sums to 2,000. The vector Population could then be created as a mixed array of data and imputations, which are both integers.

STAN can't sample discrete parameters, but this form of model specification should allow STAN to sample the Dirichlet in continuous parameter space.

Is this kind of model specification possible in STAN? It does not appear to be, given the way the multinomial is defined in the STAN language (N calculated under the hood).

Can anyone tell me if this kind of model can or cannot be fit in STAN, and why or why not?

Thanks,
