>
> I am wondering if it is possible to impute missing sample sizes (integers) for use in binomial densities in STAN.

> To explain the issue:
> Lets assume we want to know how the prevalence of a disease varies as a function of distance to the nearest urban center.
>
> Say for instance we have a population living on a reserve and from census data we know that there are 6,000 individuals
> living in the reserve, distributed across 50 villages. Further, we know from anthropological studies the village-level
> population of 40 of these villages (say 4,000 people in total). Thus, we know that 2,000 individuals are distributed
> across the remaining 10 villages, but we don't know the exact population per village. Finally, we have count data on the
> number of cases of infections per village reported by the municipal hospital, and data on the distance between each
> village and the nearest urban center.
>
> Ideally, were would like a model like:
>

> *number.infected* ~ binomial( *Population*, inv_logit(*Theta*) )
>
> where *Theta* is modeled as a function of distance to the nearest urban center.
>
> This raises some issues in STAN, however, since we need *Population* to take only integer values, but we have to impute
> missing population sizes

Right -- you can't code the unknown population value
as an integer parameter because Stan doesn't support
integer parameters.

And because it's a population size, you presumably can't
marginalize it out using summation.  (Maybe you could do
something analytical.)

> What seems plausible is using a Dirichlet distribution of length 10, to estimate how the remaining 2,000 people should
> be allocated across the remaining 10 districts. This vector could serve as a prior for a multinomial distribution of
> size N=2,000, which would transform the unit simplex into a vector of integers that exactly sums to 2,000. The

> vector*Population* could then be created as a mixed array of data and imputations, which are both integers.

You can code this, but it won't do what you expect.

> STAN can't sample discrete parameters, but this form of model specification should allow STAN to sample the Dirichlet in
> continuous parameter space.

You can, but how do you set the parameter alpha for
the Dirichlet?  The problem's going to be connecting
that to the rest of your problem.

> Is this kind of model specification possible in STAN? It does not appear to be, given the way the multinomial is defined
> in the STAN language (N calculated under the hood).
>
> Can anyone tell me if this kind of model can or cannot be fit in STAN, and why or why not?

You could actually code this up, but it wouldn't work because
by discretizing in the multiplication to create an integer,
you lose the connection to the continuous parameter and hence
lose any gradient information, which is what HMC uses to guide
sampling.

So while it might work (Andrew's been suggesting approaches like
this), you lose the benefits of HMC and turn the problem into
a random walk.  At least if I'm understanding your suggestion.

- Bob

P.S.  Very minor usage point:  "Stan" is a name, not an acronym.

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Bob!

I'm reading carefully the chapter about transformations of variables (it
contains something I overlooked. More on this in a future message) and
Ben's paper, and his message.

As to:

> In general, the
> loop for size K, arranged to exploit memory locality in column-major
> matrix storage would be:
>
>    for (n in 1:K)
>      for (m in 1:n)
>         Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * R[m,n];
>    for (n in 1:K)
>      for (m in (n+1):K)
>         Sigma[m,n] <- Sigma[n,m];
>
> It'd be even hair faster if you split the diagonal out and
> use the square() function [may not be available until 2.0],
> but the above should be sufficient.

... may I make a request?
There are a few examples in the manual (pages 101, 105, 125-126) but
they look strange to an R user. In R the inner loop of the second for is
wrong, because it would also be executed when n = K and (K+1):K is a
valid sequence in R, so m would become K+1 (out of bounds).
This is explained in the manual, but after those examples (pages 169-170).
Syntax before examples, or a footnote referring to syntax, could be helpful.
At least, at page 101 (and 105, 125-126) you could write:

for (i in 1:(N-1))
   for (j in (i+1):N)

or:

for (i in 1:N)
   for (j in 1:(i-1))

instead of:

for (i in 1:N)             // i == N looks useless, because
   for (j in (i+1):N)       // for (j in (N+1):N) is not executed

>>      y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, D * L);

> [...]

messages.body_plain:
Are you using the 1.3 release version of Stan?

We don't know of any memory leaks in any of our versions
related to anything you're doing.

I tried it using 1.3 command line to reduce the number
of moving parts and it allocated 9.3GB up front,
but didn't continue to allocate memory after that.  It
may look gradual to you if you don't have 16GB of
free memory.

I'm not clear from looking at the model or it's 2MB
data file why the memory usage would be so high!  So
I added a transformed data block with a print statement
to signal when the data init's complete, and the memory's
well under 1GB at the point the data's read in.

So I'm guessing it's an issue with the expression graph,
which is created in every evaluation of the model.
It builds out every operation in memory that's applied
to compute the log probability. These can add up.

So if Nmes * Npix is big, you're in trouble.  Every intermediate
expression used in that inner loop is saved as part
of the expression graph generated for automatic differentiation.

It does not appear to be a leak in that the memory
stays constant after the 9.3GB first loop.

The best way to trim them down is to share computations.
Things like not computing (kappa+eta) multiple times
or pow(gamma,kappa) multiple times.  This will also make
the code much faster.  It counterintuitively uses less
memory to write variables into a local variable array or
vector, then apply the sum() operation to them.  It's
also much faster.

Also, looking at the model, it's odd to me to see
something that looks almost, but not quite, like
logistic regression.  Usually you see 1/(1 + exp(-alpha)).
If you can convert to that form, you can use binomial_logit(Ntot,alpha)
instead of the above.  That will also save you memory and
time.  (Though binomial_logit may not be out until Stan 2.0;
I can't recall if it was in 1.3.)

Starting with --init=0, it takes about 120s for 20 iterations
on my notebook.  But it didn't get anywhere;  I'm trying a longer
run.

In general, I'd suggest starting with a smaller model or
less data in the same model, to make sure the model's fitting
properly.

- Bob

24 bytes plus the number of arguments times 8 bytes.

Yes, that's well within the variability we've seen.  Depending
on where the chains are initialized and what the random seed is,
it can more or less time to converge and simultaneously adapt
during warmup.  Usually once you get past warmup and have converged,
sampling is pretty consistent.  That is, most variability we've
observed is during warmup.

 > If so, what should I make of
> the wide variability in times?

That we need to do some more work to speed up adaptation and make
it more consistent?

> Another possibility is that the jobs interfered with each other.  *If*

> 2/3 of what I would expect with 100% utilization on all 3 threads.

Did you really mean different threads or is it different processes?
If you're using RStan's parallelism suggestions, it's different processes.

If you're talking about RStan, then it's definitely the time for all 3.
If you're going in parallel, each should report its own timing.

The reason things can go faster is the same reason they can go slower.
In 200 iteration runs, you spend 100 iterations warming up.  Warmup is
slower when it's far away from the posterior mass.  Usually when Stan's
converged and adapted, things speed up.  So it may take 100 iterations
to converge, then everything would go much faster.  You can look at
traceplots to see how long convergence is taking in practice.

the others.

They're not tuning parameters, per se.  Tree depth (log base 2 of the
number of leapfrog steps in the Hamiltonian simulations) is adapted on
an iteration-by-iteration basis using NUTS.

Stepsize is adapted during warmup, but unless you added variability on top of
that, will stay the same after adaption.

The accept_stat is the number of states in the Hamiltonian simulation that
were above the slice sampling threshold.  This is the stat that's tuned
during warmup the same way that a Metropolis acceptance rate might be tuned.
The NUTS paper has more info on how the slice sampling works.

The -1 tree depth is explained by the accept stat of 0.0.  It tried to
take a step, but that step was rejected, so the sampler quit and tried again.
(Maybe -1 isn't the clearest thing to report here!)

Hope that helps, but please feel free to followup if it's not clear!

- Bob

On 9/16/13 5:17 PM, Sergio Polini wrote:
> Thanks Ben! Thanks Bob!
> Stan is a white box now! (Well, a gray box.... but gray is better than black ;-))
>
> However, after reading:
> Bob: "L ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0);
> This is just uniform on L, which means it's effectively a no-op in Stan."
> Ben: "R ~ lkj_corr(1.0)
> is just a waste of time. The 1.0 implies the density is a constant."
> Stan manual: �45.8
> I understand that:
>
> a) before the digital revolution, one needed explicit priors;
> b) when using BUGS, one needs explicit (proper) priors;

I believe BUGS (or at least JAGS) let you skate around that problem
somehow.

> c) Stan has launched implicit (even improper) priors;

We do allow improper priors.  The implicit priors are just
uniform on the declared constraints.  These are proper if the
variable is bounded (real with finite lower and upper bounds,
simplex or correlation matrix), and improper otherwise (real,
real with one bound, ordered vectors, covariance matrices.

Stan does require proper posteriors.  And it's up to the user
of an improper prior to insure the posterior is proper.

> d) as to correlation matrices, if R is just a corr_matrix[K] (no explicit prior) then Stan picks a vector of K(K-1)/2
> unconstrained values and builds R by LKJ(1.0) transform; i.e. p(R) \propto 1 (\det(R)^{\eta-1}, \eta=1);

 From a modeling perspective, the implied distribution is uniform
over all matrices that are valid correlation matrices.

> d) as to covariance matrices, if Sigma is just a cov_matrix[K], Stan picks a vector s of positive standard deviations,
> an LKJ (\eta=1) correlation matrix R, and Sigma = diag(s) R diag(s). (Well, Stan doesn't do it, but what Stan does is
> something like it.)

Not quite.  WE just use a Cholesky factor representation for
covariance.  So that's (K choose 2) arbitrary values below
the diagonal and K exp-transformed values for the diagonal (so
they're positive).  These are then just multiplied, which
gives you a correlation matrix.  Both the K and (K choose 2)
variables are improper priors because they're not fully bounded.

> That is, I understand that if Stan didn't allow implicit priors, I had to use explicit priors for covariance matrices.
> The first candidate would be a scaled inverse Wishart. Slow!

We do plan to make this faster.

> But an explicit LKJ (lkj_corr or lkj_corr_cholesky) would be a no-op / waste of time.

No.  It's just the lkj_corr(1) prior that's a no-op, because

  lkj_corr(Sigma|nu) = determinant(Sigma)^{nu - 1}.

So when nu == 1, the result is a constant, hence a uniform prior.
You already get that from the declaration, so it's essentially
a no-op.

If nu > 1, you get shrinkage toward the identity matrix,
but you have to be Ben or one of the original paper authors to
understand the magic properly.

> Andrew Gelman wrote: "Another option is to just ditch the scaled-inverse-Wishart and use LKJ or something else."
> Well, if one wishes uniform priors, "something else" could be "nothing"!

Andrew would have you put a prior on the correlation matrix that
shrinks toward the identity (or not), then scale with a scale
vector (i.e., a vector of std devs), just as in the scaled inverse
Wishart.  Only instead of a base inverse Wishart, it's LKJ.

> I mean that I tried another model, let me call it "model 0":
>
> data { ... }
> parameters {
>    vector[2] mu;
>    cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
> }
> model {
>    matrix[2,2] L;
>    L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
>    for (n in 1:N)
>      y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L);
> }
>
> No lkj_corr(1.0), a waste of time; no lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0), a no-op. Just:
> cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
> Model 0 works, and is about as fast as models 2 and 3.
>
> Am I wrong?

On a few points.  What you have above isn't a proper prior.
You wouldn't use lkj_corr or lkj_corr_cholesky becuase
you have a covariance matrix, not a correlation matrix.

- Bob

On Monday, September 16, 2013 6:52:04 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > But an explicit LKJ (lkj_corr or lkj_corr_cholesky) would be a no-op / waste of time.
>
> No.  It's just the lkj_corr(1) prior that's a no-op, because
>
>   lkj_corr(Sigma|nu) = determinant(Sigma)^{nu - 1}.
>
> So when nu == 1, the result is a constant, hence a uniform prior.
> You already get that from the declaration, so it's essentially
> a no-op.

I think saying it has no effect on the posterior distribution would be clearer than saying it is a no-op. If nu == 1, then

lkj_corr = ifelse(Sigma is a correlation matrix, 1, 0)

but verifying whether Sigma is, in fact, a correlation matrix is O(K^3). So, it is essentially no-op after doing an expensive operation.

Thus, omitting the

Sigma ~ lkj_corr(1.0)

does save a lot of time for large K.

Ben

This is bad.  Treedepth of 10 means the algorithm's
maxed out and is taking 1000 leapfrog steps in the NUTS
HMC simulation (each one involving a log probability and gradient
eval) per iteration.

You also see a very tiny stepsize.

This kind of thing can happen if the model's very tightly
constrained in some dimension.  It usually signals either a very
complicated model or some issue with the model specification.

Michael might have more advice here on how to diagnose what's
going on.

>> The accept_stat is the number of states in the Hamiltonian simulation that

I'd treat it as 0.  It definitely has to evaluate at
least one log probability, and that's what this is a proxy
for.

> Is treedepth on iteration i the number of leapfrog steps used for
> iteration i, or the number of leapfrog steps determined to be optimal
> after iteration i, and used in iteration i+1?

The number used in iteration i.  The depth expands each iteration
until either (a) the trajectory does a U-turn [see the NUTS paper
for details], or (b) you hit the limit [10 by default].

- Bob

This is very, very bad.  I wouldn't trust any of your results in the slightest.

At the very least you'll have to expand the maximum tree depth until you're
no longer saturating the maximum.  Also you'll want to look at the elements
of the mass matrix -- if the step size is really small and you're hitting the
max tree depth then there's either (a) huge ill-conditioning that the
adaptation is taking too long to find or (b) huge off-diagonal elements
for which the default NUTS algorithm is not particularly suited.

I'm going to go folk theorem here -- simplify your model until you have
something that fits decently and then add the complex bits until you
start to identify where the fits go crazy.

>>> were above the slice sampling threshold.  This is the stat that's tuned
>>> during warmup the same way that a Metropolis acceptance rate might be tuned.
>>> The NUTS paper has more info on how the slice sampling works.

>>> take a step, but that step was rejected, so the sampler quit and tried again.
>>> (Maybe -1 isn't the clearest thing to report here!)

This is an artifact of the old implementation.  It should not occur in 2.0.

Sorry, I'm somewhat confused.
When I define a constrained parameter, Stan transforms it to an
unconstrained variable, then the C++ class (the one the model is
converted to) transforms the parameter from unconstrained to constrained
(and applies the appropriate Jabobian).
I suppose that the second transformation (from unconstrained to
constrained) implies verifying the constraints.
I also suppose that this happens at least n.chains x n.iterations times,
i.e. at least as many times as the number of sampled values. "At least"
because some values are rejected.

matrix?

corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
Sigma ~ lkj_corr(1.0);

sampling statement. But I can't believe it.
Please, what am I missing?

Sergio

matrix from a uniform distribution, I'd start with K(K-1)/2
unconstrained values, then I'd transform them by tanh(...) and use them

matrix (Manual, p. 273).

correlation matrix, if such a matrix is sampled from a uniform
distribution when eta = 1, what should I check?

>
>
> This is very, very bad.  I wouldn't trust any of your results in the slightest.

This used to seem very mysterious to me, so let me try
to elaborate.

The basic idea is that if each iteration doesn't go all
the way out to a U-turn, then the sampler reverts to a random
walk.  Random-walk Metropolis mixes very slowly for most
complicated models.

> At the very least you'll have to expand the maximum tree depth until you're
> no longer saturating the maximum.

That should be more efficient than the random walk you get from
truncating.

We had a long discussion up front about whether to truncate the
treedepth or not, with Andrew being pro, Matt being con, and the
rest of us shrugging our shoulders, not being able to decide whether
random-walk Metropolis or an effecctively infinite loop was better.

> Also you'll want to look at the elements
> of the mass matrix --

This is the varying step size part.  It gives you the step size
multiplier for each dimension.

> if the step size is really small and you're hitting the
> max tree depth then there's either (a) huge ill-conditioning that the

Ill conditioning means the sampler is much more constrained in
one direction compared to others.

> adaptation is taking too long to find or (b) huge off-diagonal elements
> for which the default NUTS algorithm is not particularly suited.
>
> I'm going to go folk theorem here -- simplify your model until you have
> something that fits decently and then add the complex bits until you
> start to identify where the fits go crazy.

Andrew's folk theorem is that if you have computational problems,
it could very well signal a problem with the model, not the
computation.  (He developed his "theorem" before Stan -- it wasn't
a retrofitted excuse.)

- Bob

> Il 17/09/2013 00:52, Bob Carpenter ha scritto:
>>
>> On 9/16/13 5:17 PM, Sergio Polini wrote:
>>> [...]
>>> Andrew Gelman wrote: "Another option is to just ditch the
>>> scaled-inverse-Wishart and use LKJ or something else."
>>> Well, if one wishes uniform priors, "something else" could be "nothing"!
>>
>> Andrew would have you put a prior on the correlation matrix that
>> shrinks toward the identity (or not), then scale with a scale
>> vector (i.e., a vector of std devs), just as in the scaled inverse
>> Wishart.  Only instead of a base inverse Wishart, it's LKJ.
>
> I'm wondering about what happens when I declare R as a corr_matrix and Sigma as a cov_matrix.
> The Manual says that "If no prior is specified for a parameter, it is implicitly given a uniform prior on its support"
> (page 7).

That's exactly what happens for all variable types.

> I can easily figure out what that means for scalar parameters.

Same thing happens for non-scalars, just in more dimensions :-)

> As to corr_matrix, I can imagine that something like the "correlation matrix inverse transform" (p. 273) is used, i.e.
> that the LKJ transform (with eta=1) is used.

Sections 45.8 and 45.9 define the exact transforms we use.

There's no "eta=1" in the transform.  It's just a mapping
from (N choose 2) variables for correlation and (N choose 2) + N
variables for covariance matrix, with the Jacobian adjustment.

The result is a uniform distribution.

>
> But how does Stan give a uniform distribution to a cov_matrix?
> I can't find any answers in the Manual.

Section 45.9.

Short answer is a that we use a Cholesky factor as the basis,
which requires a positive diagonal.  So there's the exp()
(inverse) transform for the positivity then the L * L'
transform to turn it into a covariance matrix.  Then we compute
the Jacobian matrix of the transform, then take it's determinant,
and that's the adjustment.

> Does just picking unbounded (K choose 2) + K exp-transformed values give a uniform prior to a cov_matrix?

Not without the Jacobian adjustment explained in section 45.9.

> When I say that "something else could be nothing", I mean that if Stan really gives a uniform distribution to a
> corr_matrix and to a cov_matrix, why bother?

Well, you might want a more informative prior for correlation
matrices with shrinkage toward the identity matrix.  For
covariance matrices, you may want a proper prior.

> As to corr_matrix, using LKJ would just make explicit the implicit LKJ transform (perhaps...).

??

The LKJ transform is always implicit for correlation matrices
in the background.  This isn't the same as their distribution,
though it's related.

> As to cov_matrix, using:
> Sigma <- diag(std devs) * lkj_corr(1.0) * diag(std devs)
> would just make explicit... what else?

If Omega is your correlation matrix, then

    Sigma <- diag(sigma) * Omega * diag(sigma)

[not the best way to implement it] gives you a covariance
matrix.  It then lets you put an independent prior on
Omega (we recommend shrinking to an identity matrix),
and on sigma (you can use whatever priors you think make
sense here).

>
>>> I mean that I tried another model, let me call it "model 0":
>>>
>>> data { ... }
>>> parameters {
>>>    vector[2] mu;
>>>    cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>>> }
>>> model {
>>>    matrix[2,2] L;
>>>    L <- cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
>>>    for (n in 1:N)
>>>      y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, L);
>>> }
>>>
>>> No lkj_corr(1.0), a waste of time; no lkj_corr_cholesky(1.0), a no-op.
>>> Just:
>>> cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>>> Model 0 works, and is about as fast as models 2 and 3.
>>>
>>> Am I wrong?
>>
>> On a few points.  What you have above isn't a proper prior.
>> You wouldn't use lkj_corr or lkj_corr_cholesky becuase
>> you have a covariance matrix, not a correlation matrix.
>
> Sure, but I was trying to say that model 0 and a revised model 2 (say model 2.1):
>
> data { ... }
> parameters {
>    vector[2] mu;
>    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma;
>    corr_matrix[2] R;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    cov_matrix[2] Sigma;
>    matrix[2,2] D;
>    D <- diag_matrix(sigma);      // needed below
>    Sigma[1,1] <- sigma[1] * sigma[1];
>    Sigma[2,1] <- R[2,1] * sigma[2] * sigma[1];
>    Sigma[1,2] <- Sigma[2,1];
>    Sigma[2,2] <- sigma[2] * sigma[2];
> }
> model {
>    matrix[2,2] L;
>    matrix[2,2] Chol;
>    L <- cholesky_decompose(R);
>    Chol <- D * L;
>    for (n in 1:N)
>      y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, Chol);
> }
>
> are not that different.

It's slightly differently scaled, because the covariance
matrix that multi_normal_cholesky uses here will be Chol * Chol'.

Why are you creating Sigma here?  You're not using it.

> I get very similar results, so I'd think that model 2.1 just makes explicit what is implicit in model 0.
> But model 2.1 is really faster. Why?

It doesn't need to do the decomposition.  It'd be even faster to
just straight-up parameterize the Cholesky factor.

> Perhaps:

> a) either model 0 gives Sigma a uniform prior in another, (undocumented and) less efficient, way;

If you find something not documented, let us know.

The transforms are ALL documented in chapter 45.

 > b) or model 2.1 uses some manual optimizations that could eventually be embedded in the code model 0 is translated to.

We are going to work on efficiency, but that won't change model
behavior.

- Bob

On 9/17/13 5:16 AM, Sergio Polini wrote:
> Sorry, I'm somewhat confused.
> When I define a constrained parameter, Stan transforms it to an unconstrained variable, then the C++ class (the one the
> model is converted to) transforms the parameter from unconstrained to constrained (and applies the appropriate Jabobian).

Other way around.  Stan does the inverse transform from
unconstrained to constrained.  That lets HMC/NUTS sample
in the unconstrained space.

> I suppose that the second transformation (from unconstrained to constrained) implies verifying the constraints.

Again, other way around.  The map from unconstrained to constrained
is defined to satisfy the constraints.  But when you provide initial
values, we have to first verify the constraint then transform to
unconstrained.

> I also suppose that this happens at least n.chains x n.iterations times, i.e. at least as many times as the number of
> sampled values. "At least" because some values are rejected.

The transform happens every leapfrog step of every iteration.

I tried to lay this out in the block execution section. There
are even tables of what gets executed when.  (Figure 23.1,
page 179).

>
> Doesn't it happen when I define a matrix as a covariance or correlation matrix?
> What you are saying looks to me like you were saying that if I write:
>
> corr_matrix[K] Sigma;
> Sigma ~ lkj_corr(1.0);
>
> Stan checks Sigma twice, because Sigma would be checked even without the sampling statement. But I can't believe it.

What happens here is that the transform from unconstrained
to constrained gets run every time if Sigma is a parameter.

> Please, what am I missing?
>
> Thanks
> Sergio
>
> PS: A minor point. If I were Stan, if I had to sample a correlation matrix from a uniform distribution, I'd start with
> K(K-1)/2 unconstrained values, then I'd transform them by tanh(...) and use them to define a K x K matrix z, then I'd
> bijectively map z to a correlation matrix (Manual, p. 273).

Not quite.  Check out the actual definition in the manual.
We do something like that, though it's trickier for correlation
matrices than for covariance matrices because of the unit
diagonal constraint.

> If the LKJ transform works as intended, i.e. if z is mapped into a true correlation matrix, if such a matrix is sampled
> from a uniform distribution when eta = 1, what should I check?

Not sure what you mean here.  What goes on under the hood is
not sampling from a correlation matrix uniformly.  What goes
on is that unconstrained variables are converted to constrained
and the appropriate Jacobian adjustment applied, which guarantees
that it's uniform.

It might help to work through changes of variables for positive
constraints and see how that works, then maybe work your way up
through simplexes, which are the simplest multivariate transform.

The LKJ transform works.  :-)

>

> I can't find any answers in the Manual.

> Does just picking unbounded (K choose 2) + K exp-transformed values give
> a uniform prior to a cov_matrix

Perhaps it would clarify to say that a jointly uniform distribution for a correlation matrix of order K is proper. Think about putting all correlation matrices (square, symmetric, positive definite, unit-diagonal) of order K into an urn and picking one out.

A jointly uniform prior for a covariance matrix would be improper basically because a uniform prior (over the positive reals) on a variance is improper. So, we can't really write down a useful expression for that. In some cases (multivariate normals), it is known that in improper prior on a covariance matrix nevertheless yields a proper posterior distribution (which Stan needs). But in general, that might not be true.

Ben

> I thought the adaptation on the mass matrix (just the  diagonal) would

That assumes the adaptation converged to the true variances.  Models
that don't mix well stress the adaptation.

> If step size is x and there are k leapfrog steps, does that mean each
> individual leapfrog step is size x or x/k?  How does the mass modify
> that?

Each leapfrog is x, so the total time integrated is x * k.  The mass matrix
scales the update of the parameters, so some parameters might move more
in each iterations while some might move less.

> Would it be worth trying allowing non-zero off-diagonal mass elements?

My guess is that if you can't adapt to a diagonal mass matrix, you won't
have much luck with an off-diagonal mass matrix.  This is where having a
simpler model and building up helps.

> The current model has interactions with respondent race (3 categories)
> for every term.  The correlations between many terms are substantial
> as a result.  Is there a chance that changing the basis of the
> contrasts could help?

Matt trick, Matt trick, Matt trick.  See the manual under "Reparameterizations".

> I'm working off the development version of rstan.  Is that 2.0 enough?

That should be enough.  I think the only way that should happen is if the sampler bails upon
encountering a NaN.

I've been meaning for ages to write a mixture model like this
for Mechanical Turkers who submit completely random results.
It's a little more complicated in that there's no official answer
key, but not much.  It's why I recommended checking out the
Dawid and Skene (1979) model.  Maybe Lee and Wagenmkaers get to it later.

> Purpouse of the model is to separate exam results who were just guessing from those who have some knowledge.

Why use a (0,1)-truncated normal rather than a Beta
distribution for a chance-of-success parameter?

Even if I did use a Gaussian, I wouldn't recommend
the gamma(0.001,0.001) prior.

> My model (below) is working and doing the job, but I'm not sure about some parts of the code. Esspecialy in generated
> quantities block - if I transformed lp__ for mixture in the right way.

You need the Jacobian for the 1/x^2 transform transform.

> The mixing actually differs slightly from mixing
> I have in Jags.

Nor surprising.  You're also missing the index on your log prob
sums.  But I'm recommending just putting it in the model and
using our log_sum_exp op.  See below.

> Isn't there a better way how to extract mixing proportions? And any other suggestions how to improve the model?
>
> I've also encountered one minor error when I was trying to put truncation on sampling of phi: phi ~
> normal(mu,sigma)T[0,1]. Stating : no matches for function name="normal_cdf" ... lower bound in truncation type does not
> match sampled variate in distribution's type .   Why is that?

in the way we're evaluating.  We need a better error message.

Specific domments on the code below.

> /model ="/

> /    lp_for_z[i,2] <- exp(log(mix[i,2]) + binomial_log(k[i],n,.5));/

See below.

> /}/

> /  mu ~ beta(1,1)T[.5,1];/
> /  lambda ~ gamma(.001,.001);/

This is where you need the Jacobian adjustment.

log | d/d.lambda 1 / sqrt(lambda) |

= log(1/2 lambda^{-3/2})   // lambda > 0

= log(1/2) - 3/2 log(lambda)

and we can drop constants, so that's

    lp__ <- lp__ - 1.5 * log(lambda);

But you should really use a different prior altogether
here.  The 0.0001 business is just a (failed)
attempt to provide a "non-informative" prior.
The simplest thing to do is just constrain sigma
to a (reasonable) interval (not [0,10000] for this
model, where the sd can't be large because
of the truncation!).

> /  phi ~ normal(mu,sigma);  # !!!/

Here you need to loop over p.

   for (n in 1:p)
     phi[p] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[0,1];

I think it'd also make sense (actually not --- the whole
use of normal here is funny) to truncate to [0.5,1].

But really, just use a Beta prior!

> /
> /
> /  for (i in 1:p) {/
> /    lp__ <- lp__ + log(sum(lp_for_z));/

You need the index lp_for_z[i] here and it should be right.
I assume this is a typo given that you had the loop.

The transformed params you had are these, but I'd just
get rid of them altogether:

   > for (i in 1:p) {/
   > /    lp_for_z[i,1] <- exp(log(mix[i,1]) + binomial_log(k[i],n,phi[i]));/
   > /    lp_for_z[i,2] <- exp(log(mix[i,2]) + binomial_log(k[i],n,.5));/
   > /  }/

Instead, replace the above loop with

for (i in 1:p)

   lp__ <- lp__ + log_sum_exp(log(mix[i,1]) + binomial_log(k[i],n,phi[i]),

                              log(mix[i,2]) + binomial_log(k[i],n,.5));

It's more arithmetically stable.  You can assign the inner terms
to a local variable if you think it's clearer.

> /  }/
> /}/
> /generated quantities {/
> /  vector[p] prob;/
> /  int<lower=0,upper=1> z[p];/
> /  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[p] theta;/
> //
> /  for (i in 1:p) {/
> /    prob[i] <- lp_for_z[i,1] / (lp_for_z[i,1] + lp_for_z[i,2]);/
> /    z[i] <- bernoulli_rng(prob[i]);/
> /    theta[i] <- (z[i] == 0) * .5 + (z[i] == 1) * phi[i];/
> /  } /
> /}"/

You can do this, but it's more efficient for downstream inference
if you just work with the expectations for z. (See the Rao-Blackwell
theorem.)

- Bob

messages.subject: RStan memory trivia
messages.subject_clean: RStan memory trivia
messages.body_plain:
I had sflist the result of 3 parallel runs of my model, and
r4 <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)

r3b was the result of a similar operation.

The process was just over 2G.

save(r3b, r4, sflist, file="r4.rdata")

Surprise #1: the resulting file is 1.8G, which doesn't seem like much
compression.

In another process I

load(file="r4.rdata")

Surprise #2: The new process is just under 4G.

I assume what's going on here is that R tries not to make unnecessary
copies, and so r4 and sflist share most of their memory.  But then when
it's written out this association is lost, effectively doubling the
size.

If this theory is right, it seems R could do better.

R 2.15

Ross Boylan

In general, it's usually more informative to

the same.  As a start, make sure the chains all wind up with roughly

> ...

>>

>> that won't converge until the other parameters have converged (though
>> it can, especially if the model's unidentifiable or only weakly identified
>> by priors).
>
> For the first chain traceplot is dominated by the first few steps
> being way off.  Tossing them to allow closer inspection suggests the
> chain doesn't get in range til about iteration 500 (of 2000).
>
> The value is not constant after that, but bounces around a
> range--which I think is what is expected.

Right.

> It shows high
> autocorrelation, which perhaps is not expected if the Hybrid MC is
> working well?

Ideally, there's no autocorrelation and n_eff = number of iterations.
But that rarely happens.  See below for a bit more on why.

> The second chain settles down some after 500, but appears to be
> trending down throughout.  By my inexperienced eye it may not have
> converged.

> The third chain appears to have converged for iterations 400-1800, but
> then seems to be heading up at the end.

These are both bad and the reason Andrew wanted the split-R-hat
he and Kenny Shirley developed.  If one chain is trending up and another
trending down during sampling, R-hat should not be good.

> All 3 have high autocorrelation.

Sometimes that's inevitable with HMC.  HMC is rotation invariant,
but not scale invariant.  The diagonal mass matrix (varying step sizes
in 1.3) just adjusts the scales per dimension.  The result is then neither
technically rotation nor scale invariant.  You need a full mass matrix
to deal with full generality.

But even that's still only a global adaptation.  If you look at the funnel
example in the manual, you'll see a simple example of a hierarchical model where
the posterior scale varies dramatically by position.  That we can't adapt
to.

Riemann-Manifold HMC will do everything here at the cost of some fairly
expensive matrix operations (solving, essentially) that apply to
a P x P matrix, where P is the number of parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: Error in call to cholesky decomposition; require symmetric matrix
messages.body_plain:
Not totally sure why your original way of doing it was causing you to lose so much precision, but evidently it did at least for one proposed set of parameters.

As to why it is the case that the Cholesky factor of a covariance matrix is equal to the product of a diagonal matrix of standard deviations and a Cholesky factor of a correlation matrix, that is just the way it is. So, basically the solution worked by doing a Cholesky decomposition of the correlation matrix (which still had good precision and thus passed the symmetry check) and then pre-multiplying to get the Cholesky factor that would result (at least if there were infinite precision) if you first multiplied the correlation matrix from both sides by the diagonal matrix of standard deviations and then took the Cholesky factor of the result.

Ben

On 9/17/13 5:45 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Tue, Sep 17, 2013 at 09:59:45PM +0100, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>> The step sizes ended up with close to 3:2 variation; is that considered "rougly the same"?
>>>
>>> Sizes were 0.0004937197, 0.0005428345, 0.000760579.
>>>
>>> Is it reasonable to look at step size without considering mass?
>>
>> Not really.  But if the step sizes are this low AND the elements of the mass matrix are roughly the same then you must have huge correlations that a diagonal mass matrix will not help.  If you're building a hierarchical model then you really should look at the Matt trick.
>
> I tried it, and am trying to interpret the diagnostics.  It took about
> twice as long as my non-trick version, though since the seed is random
> (now fixed) that may not mean much.

Is this measured in n_eff / time?  We only really care about
the rate of producing effective samples.

Basic time per iteration should be about the same.

> The step size was 5 to 7 x bigger
> than any of the ones above, which I guess is progress.  treedepth
> still maxed out.

You need to expand treedepth until it doesn't max out to investigate
what's going on.  This is indicative that the HMC dynamics wasn't run
long enough.  It may slow down iterations even further, but it's going
to be

>> tail(get_sampler_params(r)[[1]])
>         accept_stat__  stepsize__ treedepth__
> [195,]     0.8915498 0.003433122          10
> [196,]     0.8669619 0.003433122          10
> [197,]     0.8636663 0.003433122          10
> [198,]     0.9534177 0.003433122          10
> [199,]     0.7526947 0.003433122          10
> [200,]     0.6689675 0.003433122          10
>
>
> I set some of the priors arbitrarily; perhaps I need to add them as
> parameters?  In particular, I simply set the beta sd to 5.

It can make a difference if you have too wide a prior.

> The estimated sd of the cluster parameters is tiny:
>       Min.   1st Qu.    Median      Mean   3rd Qu.      Max.
> 0.0000394 0.0078710 0.0201600 0.0279500 0.0437700 0.1239000
> which seems substantively implausible.  OTOH there are 5 of these per
> cluster (one for each possible categorical outcome)  and without
> priors they are only determined up to a constant.

Is that the parameter group that has a prior sd of 5?

What this can mean is that if you have a hierarchical model, it
wants to fully pool because there's not enough data to separate
the entries.

> Many clusters are singletons and almost all will lack one or more of
> the partner race categories.   There is some degeneracy lurking
> there.  A singleton is the simplest case: set alpha[k] = Infinity and
> for k the race of the partner and alpha[j] = -Infinity for j != k and
> you've fit the data perfectly.  Maybe that's screwing things up.

This is definitely an issue.  If the model is separable in this
sense, then you need stronger priors to control the alpha value.

- Bob

>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of partners
>     int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race
>         // K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
>     int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates
>     int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N];  // partner race
>     int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of respondents
>     int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
>     row_vector[J] x[N];  // covariates
> }
> parameters {
>      matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
>      vector[K] alpha_raw[NCLUSTER]; // cluster effects
>      real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>      matrix [J, K] beta;
>      vector[K] alpha[NCLUSTER];
>      for(ir in 1:J)
>         beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*5;
>      for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
>        alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i]*sigma;
> }

You don't need to put these in the transformed
parameters block, which will cause them to be written out
each iteration.  You can make them local variables in the model.

> model {
>      vector[K] beta_x;
>      sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>      for(ir in 1:J)
>         beta_raw[ir] ~ normal(0, 1);
>      for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
>        alpha_raw[i] ~ normal(0, 1);

These can be vectorized to just

    beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);

and

    alpha_raw ~ normal(0,1);

>      for(n in 1:N) {
>        beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)'+alpha[iCluster[n]];
>        pEthnic[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta_x);
>      }
> }

It won't matter for speed, but Stan lets you put that beta_x
expression inside categorical_logit (unlike BUGS, but like
JAGS in that respect, I believe).

- Bob

On 9/18/13 3:00 AM, Sergio Polini wrote:
> Thanks Bob. Probably this matter is beyond my means.
> Let me just say that chapter 45 doesn't mention uniform distributions at all ;-)

It's implicit.  It tells you the Jacobian adjustment that
gets applied, the result is uniform.  I wrote it up with respect
to transforming a general distribution, but you can take that
to be uniform, which is what happens if none is specified.

(It's all just a side effect of applying the Jacobian.  There's
no extra code other than the Jacobian computation.  You might look
at the code to see how it's realized concretely in some simple
cases like positive constraints.)

>
> Stan has a uniform distribution on covariance matrices that does not exist in BUGS (page 300).

There's not a distribution per se, but if you declare
a covariance matrix and don't give it a prior, the
result is an improper uniform prior.

> I just wonder if I could use that uniform distribution.
> BUGS must give an explicit prior to a covariance matrix.
> What if I do not give an explicit prior when using Stan?

That depends if the posterior's proper.  If the posterior's
improper, we try to diagnose it and print out a message.

If the posterior's proper, you get samples and finite R-hat
values.

> There could be a problem: an implicit uniform prior on covariance matrices is not a proper one.
> A posterior will be proper if all priors are proper, could be improper if some priors are improper. But "there is no
> general way to check if a posterior distribution is improper" (page 301).

Well, the general way is to integrate the density and
see if it's finite.  But that's hardly an algorithm.
Stan's diagnostics are based on getting infinite estimates
for this integral as it goes.

There are ways to check for various distributions, though.

> Say that I rewrite to Stan the BUGS models in ARM, Ch17 (this is what I'm doing) and I do not give an explicit prior to
> a covariance matrix.

You should be giving them proper priors.  For example,
on p. 376, you see a proper prior because sigma.a and
sigma.b have proper priors (they're uniform on [0,100]).

You can rewrite all this using a correlation matrix
and scaling by a sd vector.  Or you could just code it
as is.

On p. 377, you see a model you definitely don't want
to translate line for line.  It puts a proper Wishart prior
on the precision matrix then inverts it explicitly.

You can put an inverse wishart on the covariance matrix and
use that.

> How could I understand if the posterior is proper?

Ben or Andrew would know.  If there's not a prior in
Ask Ben.  Or Andrew.   Or anyone else who understands
exponential families better than me.

> What happens if it is not?

See above.

> Thanks for your patience.

I'd like to see these models all working!

- Bob

I have coded it as is, i.e. the covariance matrix is a transformed
parameter:

parameters {
   ...
   real<lower=0> sigma_a;
   real<lower=0> sigma_b;
   real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho;
}
transformed parameters {
   cov_matrix[2] Sigma_B;
   Sigma_B[1,1] <- sigma_a * sigma_a;
   // etc.
}

As to scaled correlation matrices...

> On p. 377, you see a model you definitely don't want
> to translate line for line.  It puts a proper Wishart prior
> on the precision matrix then inverts it explicitly.
>
> You can put an inverse wishart on the covariance matrix and
> use that.

But I'd get a sloooow model! See:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/eSYa0vTelw4/5DxP-eBvKC0J
your kind reply:
https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/eSYa0vTelw4/5DxP-eBvKC0J
and Andrew Gelman's comment:

"Another option is to just ditch the scaled-inverse-Wishart and use LKJ
or something else."

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/eSYa0vTelw4/0i6QwkF1p5IJ

As far as I can understand, using LKJ means using an implicitly uniform
correlation matrix -- because R ~ lkj_corr(1.0) would be a logical (not
computational) no-op -- and scaling it.
I've done this too:

parameters {
   ...
   vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_B;

   corr_matrix[2] R;
}
transformed parameters {

   cov_matrix[2] Sigma_B;
   Sigma_B[1,1] <- sigma_B[1] * sigma_B[1];
   Sigma_B[2,1] <- R[2,1] * sigma_B[2] * sigma_B[1];
   // etc.
}

No problem.

What about "something else"? I've tried "nothing", i.e.:

parameters {
   ...
   cov_matrix[2] Sigma_B;
}

(then I calculate sigma_a, sigma_b and rho in the generated quantities
block.)

No (apparent) problem. It works, and I get very similar results.
So... why not?

I'd like to replace wishart1.bug (the model on p. 377) with two
alternative models: "nothing" (simpler) and then "lkj" (more flexible).
Because:
a) Stan has implicit uniform distributions on covariance/correlation
matrices that do not exist in BUGS. It's a plus, isn't it?
b) The (scaled) inverse-Wishart distribution is computationally
convenient in Gibbs samplers, but could be inconvenient for HMC
(https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/21BZjOp1IAg/H9CcL_4gqbYJ) and
is difficult to interpret.

Comments are welcome ;-)

Sergio

The good news is that it's already fixed for 2.0 :-)

I could replicate the bug with Stan 1.3 and this
model:

   parameters {
     vector[5] y;
   }
   model {
     y ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0,5),
                      diag_matrix(rep_vector(0,5)));
   }

It crashes and burns in the C++ compiler in Stan 1.3, but
compiles just fine in current 2.0 development branch.

The workaround in 1.3 is to explicitly use double literals,

   parameters {
     vector[5] y;
   }
   model {
     y ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0.0,5),
                      diag_matrix(rep_vector(0.0,5)));
   }

[Note the 0.0 instead of 0.]

What Stan 1.3 was trying to do was create a vector of integers,
which can't be assigned to a vector of double in Eigen, our matrix
lib.

Thanks again for reporting the issue --- we really appreciate
it.

- Bob

P.S.  I added an integer sum() to our to-do list.

On 9/18/13 1:09 PM, Sergio Polini wrote:
> Il 18/09/2013 09:32, Bob Carpenter ha scritto:
>> On 9/18/13 3:00 AM, Sergio Polini wrote:
>>> Thanks Bob. Probably this matter is beyond my means.
>>> Let me just say that chapter 45 doesn't mention uniform distributions
>>> at all ;-)
>>
>> It's implicit.  It tells you the Jacobian adjustment that
>> gets applied, the result is uniform.  I wrote it up with respect
>> to transforming a general distribution, but you can take that
>> to be uniform, which is what happens if none is specified.
>
> Let me see if I've got it (don't worry, this is my last attempt ;-))
> a) transform: when I declare a corr_matrix[K], Stan converts my model to a C++ class which define a probability function
> with support on all R^{K(K-1)/2)};

Right.

> b) sampling: K(K-1)/2 values are sampled from their distributions (according to that probability function);

This isn't quite how things work.  Stan just defines a log probability
density and samples from that.

The density is defined, by default, to be uniform on the support of
all of the parameters (support being defined by the constraints).

So if you declare a correlation matrix Omega, it's implicitly defining
a uniform distribution

    p(Omega) propto constant

> c) inverse transform: those values are used to build a correlation matrix by the LKJ transform and the Jacobian of the
> inverse transform.

The above, p(Omega) propto constant, arises as a result of adjusting
for the Jacobian.  If we just let everything be uniform on the (K choose 2)
basis, it wouldn't be uniform on the covariance matrix Omega.

> If those K(K-1)/2 values are sampled from a uniform distribution, it is as if the correlation matrix was sampled from a
> uniform distribution on KxK correlation matrices.

The (K choose 2) vals are what the underlying HMC sampler uses.
They're never sampled uniformly, but only sampled after the
transform.  So if y_1 ... y_{K choose 2} is the basis,
then

    Omega = inverse_transform(y)

where the transform is defined from Omega to y.

The trick is when you add another sampling statement, like:

   Omega ~ lkj_corr(2.0);

then that gets multiplied into the total probability, so
now

   p(Omega) propto constant * lkj_corr(Omega|2.0)

- Bob

Anytime something parses but does not compile, it is a bug in Stan. The debug mode is to diagnose run-time errors.

As far as I can tell, the cuts vector should be declared and populated in the transformed data block, rather than the transformed parameters block (and the same for anything else that is fixed). The compilation error happens when you try to divide by 70, and integer division is a bit fragile. I always do double division (i.e. / 70.0).

> The good news is that it's already fixed for 2.0 :-)
>

> It crashes and burns in the C++ compiler in Stan 1.3, but
> compiles just fine in current 2.0 development branch.
>
> The workaround in 1.3 is to explicitly use double literals,
>
>    parameters {
>      vector[5] y;
>    }
>    model {
>      y ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0.0,5),
>                       diag_matrix(rep_vector(0.0,5)));
>    }
>
> [Note the 0.0 instead of 0.]
>
> What Stan 1.3 was trying to do was create a vector of integers,
> which can't be assigned to a vector of double in Eigen, our matrix
> lib.
>
> Thanks again for reporting the issue --- we really appreciate
> it.
>
> - Bob
>

>

> >> poisson_log only works with int.

> >> In the end I summed manually with a loop:

> >>    int<lower=0> y[N, K];

messages.subject: rstan traceplot ignores inc_warmup?
messages.subject_clean: rstan traceplot ignores inc_warmup?
messages.body_plain:
Using the development code, with r5 created by combining 3 parallel runs
of 2,000 iterations each,
> traceplot(r5, "lp__")
> traceplot(r5, "lp__", inc_warmup=FALSE)
get me the same plot as far as I can tell, except that the background
for first 1,000 iterations are shaded gray in the first version and not
in the second.

I tried traceplot(r5, pars="lp__", inc_warmup=FALSE), but that was the
same as the second version.

As an aside, it might be nice to allow control over the vertical scale
or choice of iterations; the graph is completely dominated by the fact
that the starting values were terrible: it is essentially a vertical
line going up and horizontal line going across.  Some way to zoom in
would be nice.

Work-around:
> x <- extract(r5, "lp__", permuted=FALSE, inc_warmup=TRUE)
> dim(x)
[1] 2000    3    1
> plot(x[50:2000, 1, 1])
> plot(x[50:2000, 2, 1])
> plot(x[50:2000, 3, 1])

Substantively the graphs seem to indicate convergence, even from the
50th iteration on--a nice improvement on my earlier model.

Ross

On 9/18/13 5:16 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Anytime something parses but does not compile, it is a bug in Stan. The debug mode is to diagnose run-time errors.

Could someone send me (or the list) the model that parses but
doesn't compile?  As Ben says, it's a bug, and we want to fix
these.  They're mostly related to int vs. double these days,
and all the ones we're aware of are fixed for the forthcoming
2.0 release.

> As far as I can tell, the cuts vector should be declared and populated in the transformed data block, rather than the
> transformed parameters block (and the same for anything else that is fixed). The compilation error happens when you try
> to divide by 70, and integer division is a bit fragile. I always do double division (i.e. / 70.0).

Integer division rules are simple, and follow programming
language conventions (C, C++ and Java, anyway):

    (int/int) returns int, rounds off

    (int/real) and (real/int) return real, promoting
    int to real before divison

- Bob

On Thu, Sep 19, 2013 at 3:15 PM, Nick Menzies <nick.m...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Of note, I now get the following error message numerous times as Stan iterates through. I have checked through and cannot see how the variable fc_all takes on a negative value (it is a linear combination of things which are defined to be non-negative, unless I am missing a coding error), but was hoping that it will go away once I have gotten to the point where I can run the model with realistic inputs.
>
> Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of fc_all: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: fc_all is -1.#IND:0, but must be greater than 0
> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
>  If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.
>

The fc_all value isn't actually a negative number. In Windows, NaN is represented by 1.#IND. See: http://www.johndcook.com/IEEE_exceptions_in_cpp.html

I'm not sure why it thinks it's a negative NaN, but the bottom line is that the computation is hosed. Just FYI, the ":0" printed after the number is the adjoint value of Stan's autodiff variables.

Have you tried the print() function to see the values of:
  V1[4]*f0c+V1[5]*fic[1]+V1[6]*fic[2]+V1[7]*fic[3]+V1[8]*fic[4]+V1[9]*fic[5]+V1[10]*fic[6]+V1[11]*fic[7]+V1[12]*fic[8]+V1[13]*fic[9]
?

I'm having a trouble following the model -- I'd suggest starting with the print and working backwards. My guess is that one of the parameters above isn't initialized before it's being used.

> I tried adding epsilon() , and even 0.5 (i.e. below), to sum that defines fc_all , but no change.
>
>     fc_all <- V1[4]*f0c+V1[5]*fic[1]+V1[6]*fic[2]+V1[7]*fic[3]+V1[8]*fic[4]+
>               V1[9]*fic[5]+V1[10]*fic[6]+V1[11]*fic[7]+V1[12]*fic[8]+V1[13]*fic[9]+
>               +0.5;    # adding small pos value to see if error code goes away... does not.
>

I tried inspecting the code and following around fic and V1, but it looks like a lot of these variables are set and reset multiple times.

Some suggestions:
- Move constants like mortN to the "transformed data" block.
- It looks like V1 and V2 could be transformed data or possibly local variables declared in "transformed parameters." If so, move them. This will help with the clarity and efficiency. (This might be true for some of the other variables also.)
- Start simpler. It's really hard coming in from the outside trying to debug a model of this complexity.

Good luck. If you get past the NaN issue and are still stuck, keep us posted.

Daniel

messages.subject: Non integer values for multinomial likelihood
messages.subject_clean: Non integer values for multinomial likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am looking to use a multinomial likelihood with data that are weighted and therefore non-integer. From the definition of the multinomial in the manual it suggests it only takes integer values.

Instead (again, based on what I see in the manual), it looks like I should increment lp__ by the relevant part of the log likelihood:

for(i in 1:N) {
 lp__ <- lp__ + log( theta[i] ) * y[i]
 }

Where theta is a simplex of N components, and y is my vector of observed (weighted) data, with N components.

Does this look correct?  Sorry for the nube question, but I assume lp__ is something I could happily mess up and not notice.

Thanks - Nick

messages.body_plain:
We were discussing the value of compression earlier.  I thought a little
test I did might be of interest.

r5 is a stanfit object with results for 3 chains, 2000 iterations each,
c 1600 parameters (though it contains beta and beta_raw for the
normalized and scaled versions of the same parameters).  I'm guessing at
the number of parameters.

ls -l r5*
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2270990496 Sep 19 22:26 r5.rdata.bz2
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2106135646 Sep 19 21:47 r5.rdata.gz
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 1998663472 Sep 19 22:19 r5.rdata.xz
-rw-r--r-- 1 ross ross 2481455164 Sep 19 21:50 r5-uncompressed.rdata

Times
> save(r5, file="r5.rdata.gz")
# didn't time it, but seemed like several minutes
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5-uncompressed.rdata", compress=FALSE))
   user  system elapsed
  4.425   0.908  27.862
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5.rdata.bz2", compress="bzip2"))
   user  system elapsed
297.838   2.104 304.288
> system.time(save(r5, file="r5.rdata.xz", compress="xz"))
    user   system  elapsed
1183.858    2.600 1190.272

So compression can save about 1/5 of the space.
Times are on an i5 processor with R 2.15.  Also it's an encrypted file
system, but I don't think that affects user time.  I used the
development version of stan.

The default behavior seems pretty good; I was surprised gzip did better
than bzip2 (note bzip2 also defaults to a higher compression level).  xz
was the most compact, but much slower (20 minutes vs 5 for bzip2 and
probably a bit less for gzip).

On 9/20/13 4:19 AM, Dan Stowell wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> Just a little question - if I'm specifying some data as
>
>      vector[D] obs[M, N];   // feature data
>
> then am I correct to expect that I should linearise my values in the
> data file in the same order as a 3d array of shape [M, N, D], in
> last-index-major form?

Exactly.  It's because obs is a two-dimensional array of
vectors.  So you access the array dimensions first.

In the dump format, the data will look exactly the same as if
you had declared this:

    real obs[M,N,D];

> (Just to spell it out, this means that if D=2,
> then my vector at [m=0,n=0] has its two values actually quite far
> apart from each other in the linear format, since all the d=1 values
> are written out then the d=2 values.)

You can always troubleshoot by declaring:

     vector[2] obs[3,4];

and then trying both ways.  The wrong-way 'round will give you an error.

> The manual spells it out for a 3d array (sec 6.3) but isn't explicit
> about storage of vector or row_vector.

It's already been requested that we spell that out more
clearly, so I'm about to add an example to the manual for
Stan 2.0.

- Bob

messages.subject: Sophisticated Ways of Losing Interest: Uncertainty and Time
messages.subject_clean: Sophisticated Ways of Losing Interest: Uncertainty and Time
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

Once again, thanks for Stan!

I'm stumped with a modelling problem that feels like it would be a common one, and seems related to Gaussian processes, state space models, Kalman filters, and the other clever stuff I see people talk about on here (and which unfortunately, is a bit beyond my understanding at the moment).

I thought I'd chance posting it, in case a type of model was immediately obvious to any of the resident experts!

I suppose I have two questions:
Can anyone think of a sensible model for the problem?
Can anyone imagine how to implement my weird verbal description of a model in Stan?

Say I have N people, in J groups, who all have opinions which change over time. I have R Likert survey responses from them, say 0-20 per person, which have come in at random points in time (over say 10 years). I guess we could consider them observations of a latent opinion variable. At any given time, most individuals have 0 responses.

I'm interested in predicting the individual opinions of the N people at the present time - e.g. if they were forced to respond to a survey right now. Overall, changes in responses over time are Gaussian about 0, where the SD of that distribution increases as a function of their response(s) getting older.

Ideally, for individuals who had never responded, the prediction would be a partially pooled group parameter. For individuals that had responded, as those responses get older, the individual's estimate would creep towards the group J prior, and eventually just become it (e.g. responses have got so old that they are irrelevant).

I've hacked together a few very simple models for this, based around estimating a single real[0,1] parameter, which, multiplied by T, serves to weight an average between the group prior and the response. So when T == now, the response gets all the weight. The problem is, for those who have responded a lot, more prior mass gets thrown into their person-level estimate (an average of the weighted averages from each response), and person-estimates become less certain for serial responders, where we might expect the opposite to happen (for people with low response variance, at least).

The only other thing I can think of is an ARCH type model on individual response variance (score difference ~ time difference), used to add uncertainty as a function of time to each response, and then for each individual, multiply all their time-fattened response probability-distributions (one for each of their responses), along with the group prior, to arrive at a person-level posterior. However, I have no idea how I'd code this in Stan, and it seems a bit harebrained considering that this sounds like a problem that may have been solved before!

Does anyone have any ideas? (And if you read this far, bless you!)

> log likelihood:
>
> for(i in 1:N) {
>   lp__ <- lp__ + log( theta[i] ) * y[i]
>   }

Yes, this will treat

    p(theta) propto PRODUCT_{i in 1:N} theta[i]^y[i]

But I don't think it'll normalize properly over the continuous support.

You'll see that it has the same kernel density as the Dirichlet
distribution (the conjugate prior, so not surprising), though you'll also
see an off-by-one term there.  And you can see the gamma functions required
to normalize it.

> Where theta is a simplex of N components, and y is my vector of observed (weighted) data, with N components.
>
> Does this look correct?  Sorry for the nube question, but I assume lp__ is something I could happily mess up and not notice.

Yes, it's tricky.   Not so much that lp__ itself is tricky,
but that it's tricky to define density functions properly.

- Bob

On 9/19/13 6:04 PM, Nick Menzies wrote:
> Hi Dan, thanks for these comments,
>
> That makes more sense about the value of fc_all (i.e. being NAN).  I will hunt around and see if I can find anything
> uninitialized, though the model still runs most of the time, it just seems that 1 out of 20 iterations falls apart. This
> should rule out something being uninitialized, correct?

It seems more likely that it would be a divide-by-zero issue,
which can arise due to the "zero" being underflowed.

For instance (not an example from your code),
it looks mathematically like 1 / exp(x) would never be NaN,
but if x < -800, then exp(x) = 0, and 1 / exp(x) == 1 /0 == NaN.

Extreme initializations can put you out in places where
the model underflows, especially if there's a lot of data that
tightly constrains the posterior --- values outside of that can
be ill behaved.

> You are correct that some parameters set set and reset a number of times. The model I am trying to construct is a Markov
> model, so there is a vector that gets updated many times.
>
> For the variables that get updated many times over, maybe I should be initializing them as local variables inside the
> loop, and I will give that a try.

This shouldn't change behavior, but it's usually easier
to visually spot uninitialized variables that way.

> I definitely agree with starting simple -- I have been trying to do so but this is the moment where things have started
> to break down. Sorry the model looks like a condstruction zone, if I need to send out for further advice it will
> definitely be a cleaned up verison.
>
> Frankly, my big worry is around the autodiff: this model will do a lot of manipulation within the transformed parameters
> block, such that the values that will finally be used in the likelihood will be a <very> complex function of the model
> parameters. Is this something that might boggle the gradient calculations?

No, should be fine.  By very complex, I was talking about code
that took person-years to write, not something you could put in
a Stan file.

The biggest issue we face is overflow and underflow in gradients.

> This has been my concern all along but
> things have (seemed to have) been working so far.  I saw Bob's post on Andres'w blog the other day on 'samplers for big
> science', and though this model will be a teeny-tiny thing compared to some of them, it might be heading in that direction.

In which case, you might want to think about pulling out some of
the calculations into C++.  Stan isn't really engineered for building
large code bases --- no namespace support, no stepwise debuggers, very
weak printing and exception control, etc.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Sophisticated Ways of Losing Interest: Uncertainty and Time
messages.body_plain:
On 9/20/13 1:29 PM, Brendan wrote:
> Dear List,
>
> Once again, thanks for Stan!
>
> I'm stumped with a modelling problem that feels like it would be a common one, and seems related to Gaussian processes,
> state space models, Kalman filters, and the other clever stuff I see people talk about on here (and which unfortunately,
> is a bit beyond my understanding at the moment).
>
> I thought I'd chance posting it, in case a type of model was immediately obvious to any of the resident experts!
>
> I suppose I have two questions:
>

>   * Can anyone think of a sensible model for the problem?
>   * Can anyone imagine how to implement my weird verbal description of a model in Stan?

>
>
> Say I have N people, in J groups, who all have opinions which change over time. I have R Likert survey responses from
> them, say 0-20 per person, which have come in at random points in time (over say 10 years). I guess we could consider
> them observations of a latent opinion variable. At any given time, most individuals have 0 responses.

With response of 0--20, it might make most sense to just treat
it as a constrained continuous value, rather than, say, as an ordinal value.

You can get predictions alpha in (-inf,inf) back to (0,20) with:

    20 * inv_logit(alpha)

> I'm interested in predicting the individual opinions of the N people at the present time - e.g. if they were forced to
> respond to a survey right now. Overall, changes in responses over time are Gaussian about 0, where the SD of that
> distribution increases as a function of their response(s) getting older.

Then you can treat the alpha as varying by individual and over time in
the way you suggest.

Yes, you could use Gaussian processes for this, but it might just be
simpler to code it up as a simpler time-series model.

> Ideally, for individuals who had never responded, the prediction would be a partially pooled group parameter. For
> individuals that had responded, as those responses get older, the individual's estimate would creep towards the group J
> prior, and eventually just become it (e.g. responses have got so old that they are irrelevant).

So the value's multilevel, with a group response at a time, perhaps,
then an individual's response at a time.  Both of these could be time
series.

    beta[t] = intercept of group over time

    beta[t+1] ~ normal(beta[t],sigma_beta);

    alpha[i,t] is individual i at time t

    alpha[i,t+1] ~ normal(alpha[i,t], sigma_alpha);

    predicted_response[i,t] <- 20 * inv_logit(beta[t] + alpha[i,t]);

    response[i,t] ~ normal(predicted_response[i,t], sigma_response);

Or something like that.  It may take some index juggling if
you don't have full data of every respondent at every time.

It lets you predict going forward by having alpha[i,t] and
beta[t] for which there is no data.

> I've hacked together a few very simple models for this, based around estimating a single real[0,1] parameter, which,
> multiplied by T, serves to weight an average between the group prior and the response. So when T == now, the response
> gets all the weight. The problem is, for those who have responded a lot, more prior mass gets thrown into their

> person-level estimate (an average of the weighted averages from each response), and person-estimates become /less
> /certain for serial responders, where we might expect the opposite to happen (for people with low response variance, at

> least).
>
> The only other thing I can think of is an ARCH type model on individual response variance (score difference ~ time
> difference), used to add uncertainty as a function of time to each response, and then for each individual, multiply all
> their time-fattened response probability-distributions (one for each of their responses), along with the group prior, to
> arrive at a person-level posterior. However, I have no idea how I'd code this in Stan, and it seems a bit harebrained
> considering that this sounds like a problem that may have been solved before!

I think it'll be easier just to use a multilevel time series
in the usual way, where a parameter varies over time, with each
time increment adding noise to the previous time estimate.

Having said all this, I don't have a lot of experience in this
area and someone else probably has a better, more standard way to
do this.

- Bob

library(rstan)

data {
     int<lower=0> N; // number of households
     int<lower=0> J; // number of villages
     int<lower=0> M; // number of blocks
     int<lower=1, upper=J> village[N]; // indicates what villages each household is in
     int<lower=1, upper=M> block[J]; // indicates which block each village is in
     int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
     int<lower=0, upper=1> x[N]; // baseline value of y
     int<lower=0, upper=1> A[J]; // treatment bundle A
     int<lower=0, upper=1> B[J]; // treatment bundle B
}
parameters {
     vector[J] alpha; // village effect
     real beta;
     vector[M] gamma; // block effect
     real theta_A;
     real theta_B;
     real theta_AB;
     real mu_gamma;
     real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_alpha;
     real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_gamma;
}

     theta_A ~ normal(0,100);
     theta_B ~ normal(0,100);

     alpha ~ normal(alpha_hat, sigma_alpha); // village level

On 9/21/13 3:41 PM, Nick Menzies wrote:

> was a substantial gap between the likelihood and the model estimates, which could have created the situation you

>
> Having said that, I am planning to fit the model to data which will probably constrain some parameters very tightly, so
> I will keep my eye out for the situation you describe.
>
> If this becomes a problem, what do people think about this idea:
> 1.  Fitting the model to a subset of the data (i.e. more diffuse likelihood)
> 2. Using the point estimates (or maybe random draws) from the resulting posterior as initial values.

You can even use a direct point estimate as an initial
value, like a posterior mode.

Or you can just take a guess if you know something about
the problem itself.

You have to be careful that you start in an area near
high posterior mass.  There's a counterintuitive situation
for the high-dimensional normal where there is very
little probability mass around the posterior mean and mode.

So I'd think random draws would be more reliable.
Or something randomized around the posterior mode or mean.

> Not sure whether
> this training data should then be excluded from the main analysis, but I assume not.

Leave it in.  You still want to sample until convergence
and then run long enough that there's no measurable dependence
on the initial point.   Initializing at diffuse starting points
helps ensure you go far enough.

So even if you start from a point estimate, it can help to add
noise.  You just have to make sure to add noise on the right scale
and in such a way that constraints are satisfied.  (We're going to
make doing this automatic in the future, but we're not there yet.)

- Bob

I'm not exactly sure what the effect will be either way
or which one is the "right" one to deal with approximate
count data.  Someone should know...

I was just saying that as a continuous density it's
not properly normalized (doesn't integrate to 1).

You would need to use the the sum of elementwise products

   sum(log(theta) .* y)

Your version (as amended above) will probably be faster
because (a) you don't need to fiddle with the subtraction of 1 you
see in the Dirichlet definition, and (b) our Dirichlet implementation
isn't vectorized (in case you had multiple theta).  You do lose
error checking (parameter y must be positive and theta must be
a simplex --- you do get a check for dimensions matching in the .*).

On Friday, 20 September 2013 18:29:23 UTC+1, Brendan wrote:
> Dear List,
>
> Once again, thanks for Stan!
>
> I'm stumped with a modelling problem that feels like it would be a common one, and seems related to Gaussian processes, state space models, Kalman filters, and the other clever stuff I see people talk about on here (and which unfortunately, is a bit beyond my understanding at the moment).
>
> I thought I'd chance posting it, in case a type of model was immediately obvious to any of the resident experts!
>
> I suppose I have two questions:
> Can anyone think of a sensible model for the problem?
> Can anyone imagine how to implement my weird verbal description of a model in Stan?
>
> Say I have N people, in J groups, who all have opinions which change over time. I have R Likert survey responses from them, say 0-20 per person, which have come in at random points in time (over say 10 years). I guess we could consider them observations of a latent opinion variable. At any given time, most individuals have 0 responses.
>
> I'm interested in predicting the individual opinions of the N people at the present time - e.g. if they were forced to respond to a survey right now. Overall, changes in responses over time are Gaussian about 0, where the SD of that distribution increases as a function of their response(s) getting older.
>
> Ideally, for individuals who had never responded, the prediction would be a partially pooled group parameter. For individuals that had responded, as those responses get older, the individual's estimate would creep towards the group J prior, and eventually just become it (e.g. responses have got so old that they are irrelevant).
>
>
>
> I've hacked together a few very simple models for this, based around estimating a single real[0,1] parameter, which, multiplied by T, serves to weight an average between the group prior and the response. So when T == now, the response gets all the weight. The problem is, for those who have responded a lot, more prior mass gets thrown into their person-level estimate (an average of the weighted averages from each response), and person-estimates become less certain for serial responders, where we might expect the opposite to happen (for people with low response variance, at least).
>
> The only other thing I can think of is an ARCH type model on individual response variance (score difference ~ time difference), used to add uncertainty as a function of time to each response, and then for each individual, multiply all their time-fattened response probability-distributions (one for each of their responses), along with the group prior, to arrive at a person-level posterior. However, I have no idea how I'd code this in Stan, and it seems a bit harebrained considering that this sounds like a problem that may have been solved before!
>
> Does anyone have any ideas? (And if you read this far, bless you!)

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Ben!
I'd like to better understand that jointly uniform prior for a covariance matrix.
"I know" that:
a) inverse Wishart could be used to obtain a distribution on the correlation matrix space so that all the implied marginal densities for r_{ij} are uniform;
b) a jointly uniform prior on the correlation matrix space results in marginal priors for individual correlations r_{ij} which are not uniform.
Where "I know" means "if I've understood Barnard, McCulloch and Meng 2000."
As to cov_matrix[K] Sigma, what could be said about marginal priors for variances and (implied) correlations?
It might be a well known result, so a bare link would make me happy ;-)

Thanks,
Sergio

On Tuesday, September 17, 2013 6:55:08 PM UTC+2, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, September 17, 2013 9:14:10 AM UTC-4, Sergio Polini wrote:
> > I'm wondering about what happens when I declare R as a corr_matrix and
> > Sigma as a cov_matrix.
> > The Manual says that "If no prior is specified for a parameter, it is
> > implicitly given a uniform prior on its support" (page 7).
> > I can easily figure out what that means for scalar parameters.
> > As to corr_matrix, I can imagine that something like the "correlation
> > matrix inverse transform" (p. 273) is used, i.e. that the LKJ transform
> > (with eta=1) is used.
> >
> > But how does Stan give a uniform distribution to a cov_matrix?
> > I can't find any answers in the Manual.
>
>
> > Does just picking unbounded (K choose 2) + K exp-transformed values give
> > a uniform prior to a cov_matrix
>
> Perhaps it would clarify to say that a jointly uniform distribution for a correlation matrix of order K is proper. Think about putting all correlation matrices (square, symmetric, positive definite, unit-diagonal) of order K into an urn and picking one out.
>
> A jointly uniform prior for a covariance matrix would be improper basically because a uniform prior (over the positive reals) on a variance is improper. So, we can't really write down a useful expression for that. In some cases (multivariate normals), it is known that in improper prior on a covariance matrix nevertheless yields a proper posterior distribution (which Stan needs). But in general, that might not be true.
>
> Ben
