Hi guys, an update and additional questions.  I managed to get past the underflow problems mentioned below. Part of the solution was getting the model to a point where I was not using placeholder inputs, and the other aspect was to calculate the multinomial coefficients outside of the model. This was mainly to be quicker (only needs to happen once, and doing it in R made it easier to see what was going wrong), but also showed me that I had a problem where I was calculating log(theta^y) as log(theta)*y. It is my understanding that the later is more numerically stable, but I was getting caught by log(0.0)*0.0 --> the log(0) gave me a -Inf, that then became NAN when multiplied by 0.0.

So all good on that front.

I now have a new problem: the model is intended to have a likelihood with three components (data on different aspects of smoking behavior). When I get the first likelihood going everything seems to work fine (well, close to fine), but when I include the other two (or one of the other two), I get a problem similar to that described by Ross Boylan in an earlier post, in that the model compiles, starts to sample, and then memory usage climbs smoothly up to 8GB and then the process fails.  Any ideas?  In case it is useful, I am attaching the model script (StanScriptV30.r. I can also provide the data as well if it is useful to try and replicate the behavior.  I checked through the data for these other likelihoods and things seem fine there. It usually requires killing R to get memory usage back down to normal.

Also, if anything looks like it could be sped up let me know.

On 9/25/13 10:31 AM, Nick Menzies wrote:
> Hi guys, an update and additional questions.

Thanks for the update --- we appreciate it.

 > I managed to get past the underflow problems mentioned below. Part of the
> solution was getting the model to a point where I was not using placeholder inputs, and the other aspect was to
> calculate the multinomial coefficients outside of the model. This was mainly to be quicker (only needs to happen once,
> and doing it in R made it easier to see what was going wrong), but also showed me that I had a problem where I was
> calculating log(theta^y) as log(theta)*y. It is my understanding that the later is more numerically stable,

It is.  It prevents overflow or underflow in the theta^y term.

> but I was
> getting caught by log(0.0)*0.0 --> the log(0) gave me a -Inf, that then became NAN when multiplied by 0.0.

With theta^y, it's not clear what to do with 0^0.  R defines
the value to be 1, so log(0^0) = 1.

You can do one-time calculations in the transformed data block
in Stan.  It should be more efficient than R.

To deal with the log(0^0) issue, we have a function

   multiply_log(x,y) == x * log(y)

that returns 0 for multiply_log(0,0) for just the reason you mention.
I just realized in looking it up that we don't doc the boundary
behavior.

> So all good on that front.
>
> I now have a new problem: the model is intended to have a likelihood with three components (data on different aspects of
> smoking behavior). When I get the first likelihood going everything seems to work fine (well, close to fine), but when I
> include the other two (or one of the other two), I get a problem similar to that described by Ross Boylan in an earlier
> post, in that the model compiles, starts to sample, and then memory usage climbs smoothly up to 8GB and then the process
> fails.  Any ideas?  In case it is useful, I am attaching the model script (StanScriptV30.r. I can also provide the data
> as well if it is useful to try and replicate the behavior.  I checked through the data for these other likelihoods and

> things /seem/ fine there. It usually requires killing R to get memory usage back down to normal.

If you can send me (ca...@alias-i.com) the data, I'll look into
the memory usage.  We definitely want to find any potential memory
leaks, so it's a high priority for us.

It may not be a leak so much as just using a lot of data.  With
transformed parameters like:

     vector[4]                   out1[n_states*7000] ;  // to accumulate results.

you're going to be writing a whole lot of output, which R needs to
store in each iteration (not to mention causing a lot of memory allocation
in auto-diff).

You could try running from the command-line version, which streams
the output to file (there may be an option to do that in R, too).

> Also, if anything looks like it could be sped up let me know.

First, I'd suggest using more standard bracketing and indentation.
I find your version very hard to scan:

   for(j in 1:9) {
     ficRR[j] <- exp(BficRR[j]);    }

And you don't even need the brackets here.

Your model's a bit dense to understand directly, but if your
comment is reliable (they often aren't, which is why you always
have to read the code, which doesn't lie):

#  Calc parameters that dont vary
     zBnc_YR[1] <- 1.0;
     zBpec_YR[1] <- 1.0;
     zBpcfc_YR[1] <- 1.0;
...

then you can save a lot of space and output by defining these
as transformed data rather than transformed parameters.

Also, if you have variables that you want to use for convenience
that you don't need in output, define them as local variables.

In general, when you have repeated subexpressions, such as
(1 - fic[1]) in:

     V2[5 ] <- V1[5 ]*(1-fic[1])*(1-ff[2]) + V1[4]*(1-f0c)*ff[1];
     V2[6 ] <- V1[5 ]*(1-fic[2])*(1-ff[3]) + V1[4]*(1-fic[1])*ff[2];

it's more efficient to define local variables rather than recomputing.
Each expression takes up space and requires time in auto-diff calc,
and re-using expressions allows the calculations and space to be shared.

When you have big sums, it's more efficient to define an array, assign
elements into the array, then all the sum() function.  It saves memory
and time.  That is, rewrite:

   a <- b + c + d + e;

as:

   {
      vector[4] temp;
      temp[1] <- b;
      temp[2] <- c;
      temp[3] <- d;
      temp[4] <- e;
      a <- sum(temp);
   }

It seems like it'd be more expensive, but it involves fewer
operations (each of those + operations takes space and time,
whereas sum() is much more efficient).  Allocation, loops and
assignment are very fast and minimally sized in R.

And please please use indentation and not something like this:

     } ##### # # END OF QTR LOOP
     } ##### # # END OF COHORT LOOP
     } ##### # # END OF STATE LOOP (not implemented yet)

This:

  for(j in 1:n_states) {
     Bnc_ST[j] ~ normal( 0.0  , pri_sd  );   }    // state fixed effect

should be vectorized to:

    Bnc_ST ~ normal(0, pri_sd);

Again, it does less memory allocation internally and is faster.

And don't ever do what you did in the same place in the code, which was:

  for(j in 1:n_states) {
     Bnc_ST[j] ~ normal( 0.0  , pri_sd  );   }    // state fixed effect
     Bnc_AG1   ~ normal( 0.0  , pri_sd  );

it makes it look like the Bnc_AG1 is in the loop!  Indentation should
always always match the block structure.

Especially for programs this big, I'd recommend keeping the model
in a separate file.  I'm constantly having to select and cut models
out of R strings to run them from the command line.  And it keeps
the models outside of the code for a particular application.

This could be vectorized

   for(j in 1:12) {
     rrMort[j]   ~ gamma( pri_mort[j,1] , pri_mort[j,2] ) ;  }

by reversing order of indexing for pri_mort and writing

   rrMort ~ gamma(pri_mort[1], pri_mort[2]);

- Bob

Absolutely -- it's all about limits.

It's even trickier when you think about x^y instead
of x^x because x and y can be approaching 0 at different
rates.  And trickier still with derivatives, because
x^y is complex if x < 0 and y is not an integer;  so you
have to be careful about one-sided vs. two-sided limits.

- Bob

messages.subject: Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.subject_clean: Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.body_plain:
I'm fitting a model that parameterizes a covariance matrix.  The model works fine and converges to the true parameter values (from simulated data)...as long as it makes it past initialization.  If the initial values make the covariance matrix not positive definite, then it crashes with an error like this:

> Error : Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params d: Sigma[k0__] is not positive definite. Sigma[k0__](0,0) is 1.3203452576620608e-08.
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
>
Is this expected behavior?  I would expect that it would simply reject the sample rather than crashing the sampler.  The same thing seems to happen occasionally during adaptation, and it does what I expect--it rejects the sample and issues this warning:

> Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma[k0__] is not symmetric. Sigma[k0__][0,1] is -4.9916394362858062e+134:0, but Sigma[k0__][1,0] element is -4.99164e+134:0
> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
>  If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.
>

A little searching suggests that this was a known issue that was fixed a while back:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/18
I'm on Stan 1.3, and the fix appears in the 1.3 milestone code, so maybe the fix didn't quite get everything?

In the spirit of that issue, the minimal model still causes a crash--it's the same situation I'm facing, and the minimal model is much simpler to reproduce:

> parameters {
>   corr_matrix[100] Omega;
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   corr_matrix[100] Omega3;
>   Omega3 <- Omega;
> }
>
> model {
> }

This fails for me with the following error:
COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW.
SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
Error : Invalid value of Omega3: Error in function validate transformed params d: y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

Not surprisingly, the same thing happens if I define Omega and Omega3 as cov_matrix rather than corr_matrix.

I'm running RStan 1.3:

> sessionInfo()
R version 3.0.1 (2013-05-16)
Platform: x86_64-pc-linux-gnu (64-bit)

locale:
 [1] LC_CTYPE=en_US.UTF-8          LC_NUMERIC=C
 [3] LC_TIME=en_US.UTF-8           LC_COLLATE=en_US.UTF-8
 [5] LC_MONETARY=en_US.UTF-8       LC_MESSAGES=en_US.UTF-8

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.body_plain:
On 9/25/13 3:44 PM, Jon Smith wrote:

Is that John (like the e-mail) or Jon (like the name)
or is this a pseudonym and it doesn't matter?

> I'm fitting a model that parameterizes a covariance matrix.  The model works fine and converges to the true parameter
> values (from simulated data)...as long as it makes it past initialization.

Are you providing initial values or letting them be assigned randomly?

> If the initial values make the covariance
> matrix not positive definite, then it crashes with an error like this:
>
>     Error : Invalid value of Sigma: Error in function validate transformed params d: Sigma[k0__] is not positive
>     definite. Sigma[k0__](0,0) is 1.3203452576620608e-08.
>
>     error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
>
> Is this expected behavior?

This isn't technically a crash (my bad in the original terminology).
It's an error that intentionally terminates the program with an error message.
We do it for error checking.

The underlying reason is that if you start outside of support,
there's no good way to move into support using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
because we can't calculate gradients.

> I would expect that it would simply reject the sample rather than crashing the sampler.

That would be nice, but we have no idea how to do that.

Perhaps for random init values for covariance matrices we could
add some regularlization to help with starting in a positive
definite matrix.

> The
> same thing seems to happen occasionally during adaptation, and it does what I expect--it rejects the sample and issues
> this warning:
>
>     |
>     Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying,
>     non-fatal (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Invalid value of Sigma: Error
>     in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma[k0__] is not symmetric. Sigma[k0__][0,1] is
>     -4.9916394362858062e+134:0, but Sigma[k0__][1,0] element is -4.99164e+134:0
>     If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
>       If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the posterior.
>     |
>
>
> A little searching suggests that this was a known issue that was fixed a while back:
> https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/18
> I'm on Stan 1.3, and the fix appears in the 1.3 milestone code, so maybe the fix didn't quite get everything?

Thanks for searching and letting us know which version you're using.
And for the detailed error report below.

The rejections after initialization are due to starting at a valid
in-support matrix, then moving along the gradient too far so you're
outside of support.  That we can fix by rejecting and choosing another
direction at random.

> In the spirit of that issue, the minimal model still causes a crash--it's the same situation I'm facing, and the minimal
> model is much simpler to reproduce:
>
>
>     |
>     parameters {
>        corr_matrix[100] Omega;
>     }
>
>     transformed parameters {
>        corr_matrix[100] Omega3;
>        Omega3 <- Omega;
>     }
>
>     model {
>     }
>     |

Thanks especially for the minimial code that replicates the problem.
Sometimes it's very tricky to do, but it's hugely helpful for us,
because it's the first thing we try to do when faced with huge user
models.

You shouldn't need the transformed parameters block here to
recreate the init errors.

>
> This fails for me with the following error:
>
> |
> COMPILING THE C++ CODE FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW.
> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'test_model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
> Error : Invalid value of Omega3: Error in function validate transformed params d: y is not positive definite. y(0,0) is 1.
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done

I take it that's with automatic inits?  We definitely need
to make initialization for correlation matrices more robust.

One thing we can do is relax the stringency of the positive-definiteness
test.  Floating-point is such a pain.  With real values, we would
be guaranteed positive definiteness, but the rounding errors accumulate,
especially in high dimensions.

I'm creating an issue for it:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/240

We've frozen 2.0, so we probably won't fix it before the 2.0 beta,
but it's a high priority because we really want multivariate
models to work properly!

- Bob

messages.subject: big multinomial models
messages.subject_clean: big multinomial models
messages.body_plain:
I added more interactions to my multinomial model and convergence got
slow and poor; I was able to overcome it by running a long time (~16 CPU
hours, although I didn't use all the results since they were too big).
I am looking for feedback on ways to do better, since the model I
estimated is not the most complex model I've contemplated.  I have two
particular strategies under consideration; there may well be others.

I somehow got the impression that Bayesian methods would be more
forgiving of models with lots of interactions than frequentist ones,
though I can no longer find any specific references for that!  P. 549 of
Gelman et al's Bayesian Data Analysis (2nd edition) says "We fit a
series of models, starting with the simplest, then adding interactions
until we pass the point where the existing data could estimate them
effectively."  It's not clear to me what criteria for effectiveness is
intended, though perhaps my experience indicates I have passed that
point with my model and data.

I've been working on a multinomial model with 5 possible categories as
outcomes.  Among the covariates are 3 category respondent "race" and 2
category HIV status (probably that will have 3 categories in the end).
I've been using the categorical_logit distribution in the beta code.

My initial model had 29 columns in the model matrix, for 5x29 = 145 beta
coefficients, as well as ~ 5 x 650 = 3250 cluster effects and 2 sigmas.
This behaved badly until I added the sigmas as estimable parameters.

The model that didn't work so great had 50 columns in the model matrix
-> 240 beta parameters.

I have 2 thoughts about how to do better.

First, although fixing the coefficients for one categorical outcome at 0
is not necessary with appropriate priors, would doing so improve
convergence?

Second, perhaps it would be helpful to incorporate more structure into
the different coefficient estimates.  Right now the model doesn't make
any allowance for coefficients being related to the same covariate.

Notational digression to clarify what I mean: Two model terms are R*H*X2
and R*H*X2 for R=race, H=HIV status, and X1/2 = covariates.  Let
r(i)*h(j)*X2 refer to the coefficient on X2 for level i of R and level j
of h.  The model currently thinks there is no more relation between
r(1)*h(1)*X1 and r(1)*h(2)*X1 than between the first and r(3)*h(2)*X2.
In fact, although we want to allow the coefficients for X1 and X2 to
vary be R and H, we generally don't have strong reasons to think they
will (esp for variations by H).

So perhaps it would be better to consider all the coefficients on, e.g.,
X1 as a family with their own mean and sd, and similarly for X2.  A
higher level process could model the means and sd's across covariates.

At first blush the second strategy would be a bit involved to implement.

Any advice about whether these or  other approaches are worth pursuing?

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

P.S. Yes, I used thinning with the long run; I guess I should have
thinned a bit more.

messages.body_plain:
Nick,

I've spent some time trying to decompose your model, but it's a bit too complicated for me to make a lot of progress (By progress, I mean verifying that the model is what you intended it to be.)

With that said, here's what I've learned:
There is no leak in the command line version. This is both under v1.3.0 and the current development branch.
With that said, in some runs, the model is taking up to 12 GB, but it's not leaking. It typically runs at 141 MB on my machine for both v1.3.0 and the current development branch, when it thinks it's actually sampling.
This doesn't really tell us what's going on with the rstan version, but I don't think there's an actual leak.
I don't think the model is specified in a way that Stan can handle it. There's a lot of trickiness going on in the transformed parameters block and its showing up in the test gradient mode. From the command line v1.3.0, add the flag "--test_grad" and you can see that sometimes there are large differences between finite diff and the auto diff. Other times all gradients are nan. That's bad news. I was able to consistently get the nan's out by moving the transformed parameter tmp into a local variable, but that didn't really solve the underlying issue. The use of V1 and V2 in the transformed data block creeps me out a bit. It's just setting and resetting those variables too many times for me to be comfortable with it. I'm also having trouble keeping track since they span across different nested loops.
I would really suggest simplifying the model and building up. If this was my model, I'd start by stripping it down to just one parameter and making sure all the data is read in properly. Then I'd add a transformed parameter and make sure that was sampling from the prior properly. I would continue to build up, running the test gradient mode at each step and verifying that the model is sampling properly.
Is the likelihood right? If I squint, it looks like perhaps you're trying to implement an alternate parameterization of a multinomial distribution, but it's hard for me to see how that's implemented correctly. In Stan, you can drop additive normalizing constants (on the log scale) when they are functions of data, but not when they are functions of parameters or transformed parameters. Have you tried implementing that distribution in a standalone model? That's where I'd start.

At this point, I'm not sure how to help you model as it currently stands. If you can break it down into a simpler model, I might be able to make more progress.

I would approach it in this order: 1) put the likelihood in a model alone to make sure its sampling from the correct distribution, 2) make sure temporary variables are scoped as tight as possible to decouple the transformed parameters block, 3) build up the model starting with a parameter at a time.

If you want help breaking down the model, we can do that on the list. I'm willing to help, I just think I'm stuck with the current incarnation of the model.

Daniel

PS. Try out the Stan emacs mode. https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode. It handles indentation and code highlighting for Stan models.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] n_eff query
messages.body_plain:
n_eff is an indication of your Monte Carlo error, i.e. the error introduced from approximating your expectations with Monte Carlo averages.
In particular, if the marginal distribution for one of your parameters has mean mu and standard deviation sigma then the Monte Carlo average
will converge to N( <x> | mu, sigma / sqrt(n_eff) ).

How large n_eff should be then depends on your application.  In inference tasks typical to our applications, the mean only needs to be known
with precision relative to the standard deviation and n_eff = 100 is a good rule of thumb.  If the absolute precision is important, however,
then n_eff might have to be taken as much larger in order to achieve the desired threshold.

If you're running the same model and just varying the data you might be running into problems with adaptation getting stuck so watch out
for the tuning parameters.  In any case, for an honest comparison by eye you should indeed re-run until all models have the same n_eff.
Any numerical comparisons can always be corrected by weighted the two samples by their respective n_eff.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] big multinomial models
messages.body_plain:
Interactions are good; sometimes it helps to assign them strong priors to pull them toward 0.

On Sep 26, 2013, at 1:16 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:

> I added more interactions to my multinomial model and convergence got
> slow and poor; I was able to overcome it by running a long time (~16 CPU
> hours, although I didn't use all the results since they were too big).
> I am looking for feedback on ways to do better, since the model I
> estimated is not the most complex model I've contemplated.  I have two
> particular strategies under consideration; there may well be others.
>
> I somehow got the impression that Bayesian methods would be more
> forgiving of models with lots of interactions than frequentist ones,
> though I can no longer find any specific references for that!  P. 549 of
> Gelman et al's Bayesian Data Analysis (2nd edition) says "We fit a
> series of models, starting with the simplest, then adding interactions
> until we pass the point where the existing data could estimate them
> effectively."  It's not clear to me what criteria for effectiveness is
> intended, though perhaps my experience indicates I have passed that
> point with my model and data.
>
> I've been working on a multinomial model with 5 possible categories as
> outcomes.  Among the covariates are 3 category respondent "race" and 2
> category HIV status (probably that will have 3 categories in the end).
> I've been using the categorical_logit distribution in the beta code.
>
> My initial model had 29 columns in the model matrix, for 5x29 = 145 beta
> coefficients, as well as ~ 5 x 650 = 3250 cluster effects and 2 sigmas.
> This behaved badly until I added the sigmas as estimable parameters.
>
> The model that didn't work so great had 50 columns in the model matrix
> -> 240 beta parameters.
>
> I have 2 thoughts about how to do better.
>
> First, although fixing the coefficients for one categorical outcome at 0
> is not necessary with appropriate priors, would doing so improve
> convergence?
>
> Second, perhaps it would be helpful to incorporate more structure into
> the different coefficient estimates.  Right now the model doesn't make
> any allowance for coefficients being related to the same covariate.
>
> Notational digression to clarify what I mean: Two model terms are R*H*X2
> and R*H*X2 for R=race, H=HIV status, and X1/2 = covariates.  Let
> r(i)*h(j)*X2 refer to the coefficient on X2 for level i of R and level j
> of h.  The model currently thinks there is no more relation between
> r(1)*h(1)*X1 and r(1)*h(2)*X1 than between the first and r(3)*h(2)*X2.
> In fact, although we want to allow the coefficients for X1 and X2 to
> vary be R and H, we generally don't have strong reasons to think they
> will (esp for variations by H).
>
> So perhaps it would be better to consider all the coefficients on, e.g.,
> X1 as a family with their own mean and sd, and similarly for X2.  A
> higher level process could model the means and sd's across covariates.
>
> At first blush the second strategy would be a bit involved to implement.
>
> Any advice about whether these or  other approaches are worth pursuing?
>
> Thanks.
> Ross Boylan
>
> P.S. Yes, I used thinning with the long run; I guess I should have
> thinned a bit more.
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel, Bob,

Thank you both for your detailed comments. I am glad to hear a memory leak is unlikely.

>From my end:
Thanks for the suggestions about areas where code could be written more efficiently, I will add them in.
Similarly, thanks for the formatting tips, sorry it was hard to go through, I will try to iron these out.
For the likelihood, your squinting is correct, this is related to a multinomial, but my data are not all integer due to survey adjustments, so I could not use the built-in function. I will look at it again.
Regarding V1 and V2 being reset so many times: is the concern that this might throw out the autodiff, or make for high memory usage?  It might be useful for me to explain what I am trying to do with the model, as that may point to better ways to approach the task: the model follows cohorts of individuals over time, describing changes in smoking behavior and subsequent mortality. In the intended version of the model there would be 5200 cohorts (52 geographical regions x 100 age categories in the start year). Each cohort is followed for 70 quarters (i.e. 17.5 years), and in any given quarter V1 and V2 represent the distribution of a cohort across smoking behavior categories. The model parameters, once transformed in a couple of ways, determine the probabilities of individuals in one category moving to another category. Most transition parameters get updated each quarter, and the distribution across categories always does, hence the need to reset the values of V1 and V2 so often. At the moment I am only working with 1 state, but that still implies resetting V1 and V2 about 100*70*2 = 14,000 times. In the innermost loop I loop through  1:70 quarters for 1 cohort, the next loop out will go through 1:100 starting ages, and the final loop (once implemented) would go through 1:52 geographic regions.  The likelihood will compare the distributions across smoking behavior categories to empirical data on the same, hence the need to record them all.  Would it change anything to define V1 and V2 as local variables? At the moment I use V1 and V2 to perform all the intermediate calculations then save the results for each quarter/cohort in an array (e.g. out1). Would it be better to directly update the values of the array?  In the end the substantive question I am trying to answer involves relating cigarette taxes to smoking behavior and subsequent mortality, and the identification strategy relies on inter-state comparisons, so the model needs to get bigger still to fulfill its purpose (i.e. build in those other likelihoods and add more states to the outer loop). I stress this issue as it is useful for me to know if I am going to hit barriers that can be fixed by improving the way I code things. Given, from both of your gracious suggestions it sounds like the coding could improve a lot, so I have hope:)
Any other ideas why the memory spikes up to 12GB, if it is normally using a lot less memory?  With more testing on my end I was able to generate the same kinds of problems by increasing the number of states (i.e. the outer loop went through 1:5 rather than just 1:1).

Thanks again - Nick

On Wed, Sep 25, 2013 at 10:59 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Nick,
>
> I've spent some time trying to decompose your model, but it's a bit too complicated for me to make a lot of progress (By progress, I mean verifying that the model is what you intended it to be.)
>
> With that said, here's what I've learned:
> There is no leak in the command line version. This is both under v1.3.0 and the current development branch.
> With that said, in some runs, the model is taking up to 12 GB, but it's not leaking. It typically runs at 141 MB on my machine for both v1.3.0 and the current development branch, when it thinks it's actually sampling.
> This doesn't really tell us what's going on with the rstan version, but I don't think there's an actual leak.
> I don't think the model is specified in a way that Stan can handle it. There's a lot of trickiness going on in the transformed parameters block and its showing up in the test gradient mode. From the command line v1.3.0, add the flag "--test_grad" and you can see that sometimes there are large differences between finite diff and the auto diff. Other times all gradients are nan. That's bad news. I was able to consistently get the nan's out by moving the transformed parameter tmp into a local variable, but that didn't really solve the underlying issue. The use of V1 and V2 in the transformed data block creeps me out a bit. It's just setting and resetting those variables too many times for me to be comfortable with it. I'm also having trouble keeping track since they span across different nested loops.
> I would really suggest simplifying the model and building up. If this was my model, I'd start by stripping it down to just one parameter and making sure all the data is read in properly. Then I'd add a transformed parameter and make sure that was sampling from the prior properly. I would continue to build up, running the test gradient mode at each step and verifying that the model is sampling properly.
> Is the likelihood right? If I squint, it looks like perhaps you're trying to implement an alternate parameterization of a multinomial distribution, but it's hard for me to see how that's implemented correctly. In Stan, you can drop additive normalizing constants (on the log scale) when they are functions of data, but not when they are functions of parameters or transformed parameters. Have you tried implementing that distribution in a standalone model? That's where I'd start.
>
> At this point, I'm not sure how to help you model as it currently stands. If you can break it down into a simpler model, I might be able to make more progress.
>
> I would approach it in this order: 1) put the likelihood in a model alone to make sure its sampling from the correct distribution, 2) make sure temporary variables are scoped as tight as possible to decouple the transformed parameters block, 3) build up the model starting with a parameter at a time.
>
> If you want help breaking down the model, we can do that on the list. I'm willing to help, I just think I'm stuck with the current incarnation of the model.
>
>
> Daniel
>
>
> PS. Try out the Stan emacs mode. https://github.com/stan-dev/stan-mode. It handles indentation and code highlighting for Stan models.
>
>

messages.subject: Von Mises from new bessel function
messages.subject_clean: Von Mises from new bessel function
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

In anticipation of stan 2.0, I've been exploring the git repo. I *think* I've figured out how to implement the Von Mises density function using the new modified_bessel_first_kind function, but would appreciate input from others if not.

So, to start, I had to figure out what the Von Mises density function is in the first place. The source for the "circular" package indicates that the density function is (in R code):

    dens <- 1 / ( 2 * pi * besselI( x = kappa, nu = 0, expon.scaled = TRUE ) ) * ( exp( cos( x - mu ) - 1 ) ) ^ kappa

where x and mu are in radians. Now, the above uses the expon.scaled=TRUE argument to bessell(), which is absent from the stan modified_bessel_first_kind() function, but I think that (again, in R):

    besselI(x=kappa,nu=0,expon.scaled=T)

is equal to:

    besselI(x=kappa,nu=0,expon.scaled=F) * exp(-kappa)

(excepting a small precision difference). So, in my stan code I should be able to do

    lp__ <- lp__+ log( 1 / ( 2 * pi() * modified_bessel_first_kind(0,kappa) * exp(-kappa) ) * ( exp( cos( x - mu ) - 1 ) ) ^ kappa )

to achieve an increment of the lp__ by the log-density of the Von Mises at datum x, correct?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:
Not quite.  The problem is that there's also a Jacobian floating around from the transformation from x to cos(x - mu).  In fact, there are an infinite number of Jacobians because the transformation has to be evaluated at every zero, in this case cos(x - mu + 2pi), so you have to increment lp an infinite number of times.  This is actually a known problem in the circular statistics literature, and it arises because we sample from a non-compact space (R^{n}) where as the von Mises lives on a compact space (S^{1}).  Any transformation between the two topologies causes problems that either end up requiring things like complex numbers.

Fortunately Ben and Marcus realized that you could sample from S^{1} uniformly by using a trick that involves sampling two gaussians (actually, it can be two of any variate defined on all of R) and then normalizing.  You should be able to just use the code they were developing for the unit_vector type (did that ever get implemented?) in 2D and augment with a the Radon-Nikodym derivative between the von-Mises and uniform-on-a-circle distribution.  Which in this case I think just reduces to the density you quoted above.

On 9/26/13 10:26 AM, Nick Menzies wrote:
> Hi Daniel, Bob,
>
> Thank you both for your detailed comments. I am glad to hear a memory leak is unlikely.
>
>  From my end:
>

>   * Thanks for the suggestions about areas where code could be written more efficiently, I will add them in.
>   * Similarly, thanks for the formatting tips, sorry it was hard to go through, I will try to iron these out.
>   * For the likelihood, your squinting is correct, this is related to a multinomial, but my data are not all integer due

>     to survey adjustments, so I could not use the built-in function. I will look at it again.

>   * Regarding V1 and V2 being reset so many times: is the concern that this might throw out the autodiff, or make for
>     high memory usage?

It won't have any effect on auto-diff or memory usage.

It just that it makes the code harder to understand.

>     It might be useful for me to explain what I am trying to do with the model, as that may point to
>     better ways to approach the task: the model follows cohorts of individuals over time, describing changes in smoking
>     behavior and subsequent mortality. In the intended version of the model there would be 5200 cohorts (52 geographical
>     regions x 100 age categories in the start year). Each cohort is followed for 70 quarters (i.e. 17.5 years), and in
>     any given quarter V1 and V2 represent the distribution of a cohort across smoking behavior categories. The model
>     parameters, once transformed in a couple of ways, determine the probabilities of individuals in one category moving
>     to another category. Most transition parameters get updated each quarter, and the distribution across categories
>     always does, hence the need to reset the values of V1 and V2 so often.

 >     At the moment I am only working with 1 state,
>     but that still implies resetting V1 and V2 about 100*70*2 = 14,000 times. In the innermost loop I loop through  1:70
>     quarters for 1 cohort, the next loop out will go through 1:100 starting ages, and the final loop (once implemented)
>     would go through 1:52 geographic regions.  The likelihood will compare the distributions across smoking behavior
>     categories to empirical data on the same, hence the need to record them all.  Would it change anything to define V1
>     and V2 as local variables?

I think it'd make the code much clearer.  You usually want
to declare something near where it's used so that it's scope
is clear and you can relate its use back to its definition.

>     At the moment I use V1 and V2 to perform all the intermediate calculations then save the
>     results for each quarter/cohort in an array (e.g. out1). Would it be better to directly update the values of the
>     array?  In the end the substantive question I am trying to answer involves relating cigarette taxes to smoking
>     behavior and subsequent mortality, and the identification strategy relies on inter-state comparisons, so the model
>     needs to get bigger still to fulfill its purpose (i.e. build in those other likelihoods and add more states to the
>     outer loop). I stress this issue as it is useful for me to know if I am going to hit barriers that can be fixed by
>     improving the way I code things. Given, from both of your gracious suggestions it sounds like the coding could
>     improve a lot, so I have hope:)

>   * Any other ideas why the memory spikes up to 12GB, if it is normally using a lot less memory?

What do you mean by normally using a lot less memory?

The only difference in memory between runs in Stan should
be how many leapfrog steps get taken.  With a lot of parameters,
this can make a big difference and may be related to the
instability Daniel was seeing in numerical evaluations.

Some of these problems we can't really fix at a deep level
because Stan lets you write arbitrary code and arbitrary code
with lots of numerical operations (like you have) can be
badly behaved.

So I'd strongly second Daniel's suggestion to move up
to a full model gradually.  He has a number of excellent
suggestions.   (We practice what we preach here!  Daniel and
I have been working on some complicated models over the past
couple of months and always start with the simplest model
we can, even if it doesn't make sense for the final problem.
It's easier to build up from things that work than it is to
diagnose something large that doesn't work.

It's usually good modeling practice to do this anyway because
it lets you compare the results of simpler models to more
complex ones.  (And no, I don't want to get dragged into
a technical discussion of model comparison --- I'll leave
that to Andrew on his blog and in the 3rd Edition of
Bayesian Data Analysis.)

>     With more testing on
>     my end I was able to generate the same kinds of problems by increasing the number of states (i.e. the outer loop
>     went through 1:5 rather than just 1:1).

What kinds of problems?

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] big multinomial models
messages.body_plain:
On 9/26/13 10:03 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Interactions are good; sometimes it helps to assign them strong priors to pull them toward 0.
> On Sep 26, 2013, at 1:16 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>
>> I added more interactions to my multinomial model and convergence got
>> slow and poor; I was able to overcome it by running a long time (~16 CPU
>> hours, although I didn't use all the results since they were too big).
>> I am looking for feedback on ways to do better, since the model I
>> estimated is not the most complex model I've contemplated.  I have two
>> particular strategies under consideration; there may well be others.
>>
>> I somehow got the impression that Bayesian methods would be more
>> forgiving of models with lots of interactions than frequentist ones,
>> though I can no longer find any specific references for that!

They should be in theory because:

   -- they don't have the point estimation problem of controlling
      hierarchical parameters to not go to variance 0 (though see some
      of the work Andrew, Vince Dorie, and Sophia Rabe-Hesketh did on
      this issue by using maximal marginal likelihood with boundary-avoiding
      priors)

   -- they take the uncertainty of their estimates into account for inference.

>> P. 549 of
>> Gelman et al's Bayesian Data Analysis (2nd edition) says "We fit a
>> series of models, starting with the simplest, then adding interactions
>> until we pass the point where the existing data could estimate them
>> effectively."  It's not clear to me what criteria for effectiveness is
>> intended, though perhaps my experience indicates I have passed that
>> point with my model and data.

It's not precise because it's a practical issue.  You need to be
able to fit the model and then you need to be able to see that the
more complicated model makes a difference to whatever inference you
really care about.  You might care about some parameter but not be
able to estimate it accurately due to either software or data constraints.

>> I've been working on a multinomial model with 5 possible categories as
>> outcomes.  Among the covariates are 3 category respondent "race" and 2
>> category HIV status (probably that will have 3 categories in the end).
>> I've been using the categorical_logit distribution in the beta code.
>>
>> My initial model had 29 columns in the model matrix, for 5x29 = 145 beta
>> coefficients, as well as ~ 5 x 650 = 3250 cluster effects and 2 sigmas.
>> This behaved badly until I added the sigmas as estimable parameters.
>>
>> The model that didn't work so great had 50 columns in the model matrix
>> -> 240 beta parameters.
>>
>> I have 2 thoughts about how to do better.
>>
>> First, although fixing the coefficients for one categorical outcome at 0
>> is not necessary with appropriate priors, would doing so improve
>> convergence?

Strong enough priors to identify the scales of the
coefficients should do the job.

>> Second, perhaps it would be helpful to incorporate more structure into
>> the different coefficient estimates.  Right now the model doesn't make
>> any allowance for coefficients being related to the same covariate.

Pooling can sometimes help, too.  Especially if there are lots of
related little groups without much data.

>> Notational digression to clarify what I mean: Two model terms are R*H*X2
>> and R*H*X2 for R=race, H=HIV status, and X1/2 = covariates.  Let
>> r(i)*h(j)*X2 refer to the coefficient on X2 for level i of R and level j
>> of h.

You seem to wind up with a multiplicative non-identifiability problem here.
If you cut all the r(i) in half and double all the h(j), you get the
same coefficient.  You can usually control this kind of thing by putting
a strong prior on either r or h and letting the other control the overall
scale.

>> The model currently thinks there is no more relation between
>> r(1)*h(1)*X1 and r(1)*h(2)*X1 than between the first and r(3)*h(2)*X2.
>> In fact, although we want to allow the coefficients for X1 and X2 to
>> vary be R and H, we generally don't have strong reasons to think they
>> will (esp for variations by H).
>>
>> So perhaps it would be better to consider all the coefficients on, e.g.,
>> X1 as a family with their own mean and sd, and similarly for X2.  A
>> higher level process could model the means and sd's across covariates.
>>
>> At first blush the second strategy would be a bit involved to implement.
>>
>> Any advice about whether these or  other approaches are worth pursuing?
>>
>> Thanks.
>> Ross Boylan
>>
>> P.S. Yes, I used thinning with the long run; I guess I should have
>> thinned a bit more.

The command-line version of Stan outputs incrementally rather than storing
everything in memory.  We should add that kind of option to RStan, too.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Do you mean underperforming in the sense of
being slower or underperforming in the sense of
not getting the estimates you expect?

By GLM you mean the R package glm?  That's not going
to produce exactly the same estimates because the Stan
model has priors and estimates using posterior mean rather
than posterior mode (which is what I'm assuming glm in R
is doing --- I don't actually know that).  So one thing I'd
check is sensitivity to the priors and then I'd do posterior
histograms of the coefficient estimates and see how they
look vs. the glm estimates.

I also saw this on the page you linked:

 > I was mostly interested in speeding up the calculation and found that,
 > with an equal number of burn-in (warmup) and
 > final saved steps, a run that took 54 minutes with JAGS
 > took 3.5 minutes with STAN. I do not claim that is a perfectly
 > fair or complete comparison. It does include the compile time of the
 > C++ code in STAN and 500 adapt steps in JAGS.

Raw time per iteration isn't important, it's time per number
of effective samples.  It's a bit hard to do a direct apples-to-apples
comparison because the effective sample size estimators differ
between R2jags and RStan (or Stan's bin/print on the command line).

You probably also want to measure time to convergence (that is, time
before you get your first effective sample).

You might also want to compare memory usage if that matters.  The
ratio between Stan and JAGS varies depending on the connectivity of
the graphical model in JAGS.

Here's the linked model:

data {
   int<lower=0> nPredictors;
   int<lower=0> nData;
   int<lower=0,upper=1> y[nData];
   matrix[nData,nPredictors] x;
}
parameters {
   real z0;
   vector[nPredictors] z;
}
model {
   z0 ~ normal(0,3.2);
   for (d in 1:nPredictors)
       z[d] ~ normal(0,2);
   for (n in 1:nData)
     y[n] ~ bernoulli(inv_logit(z0 + x[n] * z));
}

The model looks like a basic logistic regression with an
intercept.

Using bernoulli_logit (as Andrew suggested) and vectorizing
should make it considerably faster and require less memory.

   model {
     z0 ~ normal(0,3.2);
     z ~ normal(0,2);
     y ~ bernoulli_logit(z0 + x * z);
   }

Whether you think it's clearer or not will depend on how
you feel about vectorization :-)  We named "bernoulli_logit"
the way we did because the parameter is on the logit scale
compared to the usual [0,1] parameter for Bernoulli.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Positive definiteness failure on initialization causes crash rather than rejection
messages.body_plain:
The other thing you can do is just reassign to
a plain old matrix.  But that could fail when passed into
a multivariate probabilty function, which also checks
positive definiteness.

We're going to be rewriting soon after the 2.0 release
to make it much easier to work with the Cholesky factor
basis of either a correlation or covariance matrix.  This
is a lot more arithmetically stable.

 > also pass the data to the initialization function in R.

Good idea.  Today's my day for creating RStan feature requests:

https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/19

R's scope is flexible enough to let your initialization function
depend on the data if it's visible to the function.  Or
you could write a program that takes the data as an argument and
returns an init function.   I also suggested we might just provide
an instance of how to do the latter and leave the function signature
as is, because I don't know how to do what you suggest while maintaining
backward compatibility.

- Bob

On 9/25/13 6:00 PM, Jon Smith wrote:
>
>     This isn't technically a crash (my bad in the original terminology).
>     It's an error that intentionally terminates the program with an error message.
>     We do it for error checking.
>
>     The underlying reason is that if you start outside of support,
>     there's no good way to move into support using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
>     because we can't calculate gradients.
>
>      > I would expect that it would simply reject the sample rather than crashing the sampler.
>
>     That would be nice, but we have no idea how to do that.
>
>     Perhaps for random init values for covariance matrices we could
>     add some regularlization to help with starting in a positive
>     definite matrix.
>
>
> Ah, that all makes sense--thanks!
>
> Yes, this only happens with random init values.  Adding some regularization or increasing the tolerance on the positive
> definiteness check would be great.  You could also draw new init values--I know Stan does this sometimes (I've run into
> the limit where it fails after 100 failed initialization attempts), though I can imagine it being helpful for this to
> continue to fail gracefully to help in diagnosing more serious modeling problems.
>
>     I take it that's with automatic inits?  We definitely need
>     to make initialization for correlation matrices more robust.
>
>     One thing we can do is relax the stringency of the positive-definiteness
>     test.  Floating-point is such a pain.  With real values, we would
>     be guaranteed positive definiteness, but the rounding errors accumulate,
>     especially in high dimensions.
>
>     I'm creating an issue for it:
>

>     https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/240 <https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/240>

>
>     We've frozen 2.0, so we probably won't fix it before the 2.0 beta,
>     but it's a high priority because we really want multivariate
>     models to work properly!
>
>     - Bob
>
>
> Thanks for the explanation and for creating the issue.  It's certainly not a showstopper--I can still get things to work
> fine by simply ignoring the chains with bad inits.
>
> I could also be less lazy and write my own initialization function--I've just avoided it because I'm still making a lot
> of changes to my own model.  On that note, I have a small RStan idea: it would be great if, in addition to the chain_id
> parameter, I could also pass the data to the initialization function in R.  The number of parameters in my model depends
> on the size of the data, and it would be great if I could write a generic initialization function without hard-coding
> the number of parameters.
>
> Thanks again for the help!
>

Works for me.  :-)

Here's my Stan model (which is just vectorized with variable
renaming from what David originally sent):

----------------lr.stan----------------
data {
   int<lower=0> K;
   int<lower=0> N;
   int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N];
   matrix[N,K] x;
}
parameters {
   real alpha;
   vector[K] beta;
}
model {
   alpha ~ normal(0,3.2);
   beta ~ normal(0,2);
   y ~ bernoulli_logit(alpha + x * beta);
}
---------------------------------------

And here's the simulation in R:

-----------------lr.R-----------------------
library('rstan');

inv_logit <- function(u) { return(1 / (1 + exp(-u))); }

N <- 1000;
K <- 4;
x <- matrix(rnorm(N*K, 0, 1.5), N, K);
alpha <- rnorm(1,0,3.2);
beta <- rnorm(K,0,2);
y <- rep(NA,N);
for (n in 1:N)
   y[n] <- rbinom(1,1,inv_logit(alpha + sum(x[n,] * beta)));

fit <- stan("lr.stan",data=c("K","N","y","x"));

>> On Thu, Sep 26, 2013 at 01:32:18PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>> On 9/26/13 10:03 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>>> Interactions are good; sometimes it helps to assign them strong priors to pull them toward 0.
>>>> On Sep 26, 2013, at 1:16 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:

> ...

>>>>> Second, perhaps it would be helpful to incorporate more structure into
>>>>> the different coefficient estimates.  Right now the model doesn't make
>>>>> any allowance for coefficients being related to the same covariate.
>>>
>>> Pooling can sometimes help, too.  Especially if there are lots of
>>> related little groups without much data.
>>>
>> By pooling do you mean something different than I was talking about?
>

> Nope -- same thing.

Good.  So I guess I should make the effort to try this.

>
>>>>> Notational digression to clarify what I mean: Two model terms are R*H*X2
>>>>> and R*H*X2 for R=race, H=HIV status, and X1/2 = covariates.  Let
>>>>> r(i)*h(j)*X2 refer to the coefficient on X2 for level i of R and level j
>>>>> of h.
>>>
>>> You seem to wind up with a multiplicative non-identifiability problem here.
>>> If you cut all the r(i) in half and double all the h(j), you get the
>>> same coefficient.  You can usually control this kind of thing by putting
>>> a strong prior on either r or h and letting the other control the overall
>>> scale.
>>
>> The notation r(i)*h(j)*X2 refers to a single coefficient (maybe I
>> should have used a ":" instead of a "*" to fit the usual R model
>> notation better), which could be called beta[i, j, k] where k indexes
>> explanatory variables like X1 and X2.  I'm currently estimating all
>> the beta, but not individual terms like r(i).
>

> Ah --- so that's like what lmer uses for interaction terms in
> their regression notation?  I can never figure out R notation,
> but when I saw "term" I figured "*" was multiplication.
>

R models typically look like
y~a+b
meaning outcome y is a function of a and b.  If a is continuous that
means estimate one coefficient; if it is categorical, estimate several
(one can pick the exact contrast style).  Estimating an interaction is
indicated with a ":" (using spacing to make the binding clearer)
y ~ a + b + a:b
where a:b denotes the interaction of a and b, which is computed
appropriately for the measurement level of each.

The previous formula can be shortened to
y ~ a*b

where "*" means the interaction term and all lower-order combinations
of interactions and main effects.

The model.matrix() function in R creates an appropriately expanded model
matrix so that each column corresponds to one coefficient to be
estimated.  I use it to pre-proces the data before I hand it to rstan.

Before I do the model.matrix() I do model.frame() to drop rows with
missing data.

So to get the nesting we were discussing above I will need to figure
out which columns "go together" and pass that info into my stan model.

Ross

Hi Daniel, Bob,

Thanks again for the long list of great suggestions. I have implemented them through-out the code and in general they are making things a lot faster, as well as hopefully making the code more understandable.

One aspect I wanted to check specifically: you had noted that I was generating a number of large arrays (e.g. out1) which might be using up a lot of memory. The reason I had out1 was to store a lot of values in the transformed parameters which would then be evaluated against the likelihood under the model block. I have tried to get around the need for out1 by evaluating the likelihood immediately each time I generate new simulation results (i.e. each iteration of the innermost loop). As lp__ cannot be updated outside the model block (correct?) I just use a new parameter to accumulate all the log-likelihoods, then add this to lp__ in the model block.  Acknowledging this does not follow the normal process, do you see any potential problems with this?

Overall the model seems to turn over about twice as fast as before (about 4 iterations per second). However, this does not seem to have fixed the problems mentioned earlier. I seem to encounter one of two general behaviors when I run the model with a low value for iter (e.g. 100) and no thinning :

a. The model adapts quickly and then continues to sample for a long time. This seems to involve many more iterations than 100 (I print lp__ to the console once per iteration, so just count how this cycles through), and lp_ seems to gradually increase. I assume this is just the model working as it should?  I (naively) thought setting iter to 100 might mean that the model only cycles trough 100 times, but it seems this is not the case, it just seem to keep going.

b. Other times the model compiles, everything looks good, it samples once or a couple of times, then memory usage goes up to 8GB (max of my computer) and things freeze. Sometimes this will be be with the same model that worked moments ago (i..e the situation a described above). When I try to expand the model in one of the ways I had planned to (i.e. add additional components to the likelihood, or run the model for multiple states) it seems to crash every time.

Any thoughts welcome. My plan from here is to simplify the model down and see if that leads to revelations about what is wrong. Per Dan's advice, I have run a super simple model just to make sure the likelihood works, and it seems to be.  Also, Bob had an earlier suggestion to code it up in C++ and I might do this as well (with R and rcpp anyway) so I can run in with an optimization algorithm to generate inits that are closer to the posterior max, in case that helps.

Best - Nick

You can make them local variables in the model block if you
don't need to save them.

> I have tried to get around the

Also in transformed parameters, though I'd recommend only
including the Jacobian adjustments there.

> I just use a new parameter to
> accumulate all the log-likelihoods, then add this to lp__ in the model block.  Acknowledging this does not follow the
> normal process, do you see any potential problems with this?

That'll work.  But you can just move everything into the
model block as a local variable.

> Overall the model seems to turn over about twice as fast as before (about 4 iterations per second). However, this does
> not seem to have fixed the problems mentioned earlier. I seem to encounter one of two general behaviors when I run the
> model with a low value for iter (e.g. 100) and no thinning :
>
> a. The model adapts quickly and then continues to sample for a long time. This seems to involve many more iterations
> than 100 (I print lp__ to the console once per iteration, so just count how this cycles through), and lp_ seems to
> gradually increase.  I assume this is just the model working as it should?

 From random initialization, it should increase until convergence, then start
to bounce around.  From an MLE initialization, you'd get the opposite, a
decrease until convergence, then bouncing.

> I (naively) thought setting iter to 100 might
> mean that the model only cycles trough 100 times, but it seems this is not the case, it just seem to keep going.

You can set the total iterations.  NUTS controls the
number of leapfrog steps, though, unless you specify
the number of leapfrog steps explicitly, which we don't
recommend.

> b. Other times the model compiles, everything looks good, it samples once or a couple of times, then memory usage goes
> up to 8GB (max of my computer) and things freeze. Sometimes this will be be with the same model that worked moments ago
> (i..e the situation a described above). When I try to expand the model in one of the ways I had planned to (i.e. add
> additional components to the likelihood, or run the model for multiple states) it seems to crash every time.

Can you try setting the max tree depth to something lower
and see if you still get memory spikes?  That'll control
the number of leapfrog steps per iteration.

Could I ask again which version of Stan or RStan you're using?

> Any thoughts welcome. My plan from here is to simplify the model down and see if that leads to revelations about what is
> wrong. Per Dan's advice, I have run a super simple model just to make sure the likelihood works, and it seems to be.
>   Also, Bob had an earlier suggestion to code it up in C++ and I might do this as well (with R and rcpp anyway) so I can
> run in with an optimization algorithm to generate inits that are closer to the posterior max, in case that helps.

I didn't mean to suggest coding in C++!  I may have suggested
running from the command line, because that doesn't store all
the samples --- it streams them out to disk as it goes.  If you
can figure out good inits, that can help.  You definitely don't
want to be starting too far out in the tail of the posterior.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

First and foremost: I love STAN. I have found it to be a great tool, far surpassing BUGS/JAGS for my purposes and much more convenient than fresh-coding models all the time

I have a question about a model that I'm trying to code up in STAN. The data I am working with is a panel dataset with N (indexed by i) individuals an T (indexed by t) time points. The basic version of the model (and what I have gotten to work in STAN) is

y_it = w1*x1_it + w2*x2_it + w3*x3_it + w4*x4_it + epsilon_it,

where epislon is normal and the vector (w1,w2,w3,w4) ~ Dirichlet((alpha1,alpha2,alpha3,alpha4)). The w's are weights and need to sum to 1.

As I said, this version is coded and works well (and is fast).

I'm trying to do a more sophisticated version where I parameterize the w's as functions of covariates. In other words, instead of assuming that w1 is fixed across observations, I want to let w1 of each observation to be a function of covariates of its own (call these z_it). That is, I want to change the model to

y_it = w1_it*x1_it + w2_it*x2_it + w3_it*x3_it + w4_it*x4_it + epsilon_it,

where w1_it = gamma_0 + gamma_1*z_it + noise_it and so on for w2,3, and 4.

Of course I cannot literally estimate a weight for each observation, but since the gamma's are fixed across observations, I know that the model is identified. However, I'm not sure how parameterize this using a Dirichlet. I tried doing it using normals and then mapping them to the simplex using the transform exp(phi_i)/sum(exp(phi)).

Any ideas?

Best,

Adam

The question's really whether you get the same answer or
not.  We haven't investigated this issue a lot ourselves
on NUTS.

Setting a max treedepth of 5 is still sound asymptotically (so is depth
0, which just reduces to Metropolis),
but it'll wind up being more of a random walk than with a deeper bound.

Generally, Matt and Michael (the ones who know the most about
this, along with Marcus) have been suggesting that you really
want to let NUTS go as far as it wants to, because that'll be
most efficient.  Andrew, on the other hand, has argued for
lower upper limits.  So depth 10 is something of a compromise.

The real question is how to verify that you're getting the
right answer.  The danger's that you can get trapped in some
small region of the posterior and it can look like it's
converged (good R-hat and effective sample size estimates), but
it really hasn't.  So if you can run with a deeper treedepth
and get the same answer, running with a shallower one should
be OK.  Similarly, Michael's been suggesting all along to run
with a fixed lower step size than the one that adaptation finds
and make sure that provides the same answer.

- Bob

>

Thanks for sharing the particular example.  It's very much
like what I did for the ability parameters in my IRT model.

I'm very curious as to what happens to posterior inference
in these cases to the likelihood for y.  My guess is that
with fat fixed priors (scale = 5), the inferences for y won't change
much compared to a tighter prior of scale=0.1.  If they did,
I'd think beta would be more constrained by the data.

Although the posterior for beta will look very different in terms of
variance, I haven't found the mean changes much.  But you have
to run a lot more iterations to get enough effective samples because
the beta is so unconstrained.  I found with the IRT model
that if I used a very weak prior and ran for 100K iterations,
I'd get the same posterior mean for an item difficulty parameter
as running 1K iterations with a hierarchical prior.

I want a name for a model like this --- where if you run long enough
you get the right posterior mean, but where it's not so well identified
that this happens quickly.   With a truly non-identified model, it
doesn't matter how long you run, you won't get convergence.  And if
it's not identified as to scale, Stan will usually diagnose this and
halt with a warning that the posterior isn't proper because it'll try
to run the parameter off to infinity.

- Bob

I've been having some trouble fitting multinomial logit in stan and have read a few things about issues with categorical(softmax()) here that suggested there may be a memory leak?

I have a very large multinomial model that I am trying to fit: about 50 categories and a couple thousand parameters.  The model matrix is very sparse since I include "person-specific" random effect which each observation (with partial pooling on the params).  Each row of the model matrix has roughly 30 non-zero entries (out of a few thousand).  I have about 75,000 data points.

When I tried to fit this model in stan everything compiled nicely but it hung once it began sampling.  Eventually it segfaulted.

I also have a few questions about implementing this efficiently in stan.  With a very sparse model matrix, am I better off specifying response[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta*x[n]) as in the documentation, or rather should I specify eta[n] in the transformed parameters section using a series of for loops to index and sum up the relevant parameters?   E.g. in a loop something like
eta[n,k] <- eta[n,k]+beta[index[n,k]]

Finally, is it better at this stage to use softmax or to specify probs[n] <- exp(eta[n])/sum(eta[n]) in transformed parameters section?  categorical_logit will be available in stan 2.0?

Thanks,
Alex

messages.body_plain:
There are some things I don't think rstan does (using the development
version, but perhaps the help files don't reflect all recent work) that
I would like it to do.

1. extract() has options to include or exclude warmup.  It would be nice
to have an option to specify the warmup period if, for example, I run
2,000 iterations (with the default half of them warmup) but decide that
things seemed to have converged after fewer than 1,000 iterations.

Or is it not a good idea to use the warmup period, during which it is
tuning parameters?

2. It would be nice if extract() could produce a 2 dimensional matrix,
with iterations (from all chains) as rows and parameters as columns.

3. It would be nice if monitor() could be called directly on a stanfit
object.

4. A convenient method to get effective sample size would be nice.

5. A convenient method to get an overall summary of how the model has
performed, perhaps the distribution of n_eff and rhat across parameters,
would be very useful in assessing performance.  I and others have fallen
into the trap of assessing performance using time/iteration instead of
time/n_eff; I suspect part of the reason is that it is not easy to pull
out the n_effs and not obvious how one should summarize all the
different n_effs.

All of this can be obtained with suitable code; it would be helpful if
that code were already in the package.

Some of these issues are not so pressing if one has a limited number of
parameters so that inspecting the printed summary of the fit is
practical.  But even the plot() method (which does provide a quick
color-coded way to scan for bad rhat) breaks down when there are too
many parameters.

Ross Boylan

On 9/27/13 3:43 PM, Alexander Franks wrote:
> I've been having some trouble fitting multinomial logit in stan and have read a few things about issues with
> categorical(softmax()) here that suggested there may be a memory leak?

As far as we know, there's no memory leak for softmax
in 1.3 or in the coming 2.0 versions.  Having said that,
it is memory intensive (more about that below).

> I have a very large multinomial model that I am trying to fit: about 50 categories and a couple thousand parameters.
>   The model matrix is very sparse since I include "person-specific" random effect which each observation (with partial
> pooling on the params).  Each row of the model matrix has roughly 30 non-zero entries (out of a few thousand).  I have
> about 75,000 data points.
>
> When I tried to fit this model in stan everything compiled nicely but it hung once it began sampling.  Eventually it
> segfaulted.

Segfaulted or just ran out of memory with a bad_alloc
exception?  If it really was a segfault, could you send
us the output and some description of the platform you're
running on?

> I also have a few questions about implementing this efficiently in stan.  With a very sparse model matrix, am I better
> off specifying response[n] ~ categorical(softmax(beta*x[n]) as in the documentation, or rather should I specify eta[n]
> in the transformed parameters section using a series of for loops to index and sum up the relevant parameters?   E.g. in
> a loop something like
> eta[n,k] <- eta[n,k]+beta[index[n,k]]

I'm not exactly sure what the two alternatives are you're
considering or what the index[n,k] variable is doing.  Could
you share the whole loop?

In general, you don't want to be multiplying by known
0 values if you can help it.

But rather than doing a loop like this:

   real foo;
   foo <- 0;
   for (n in 1:N)
     foo <- foo + bar[n];

it's better to do

   foo <- sum(bar);

This is true even if everything's not in a simple array or vector
like bar to begin with (that is, if you have to allocate and
populate bar).  The reason is because the sum operation uses
less memory than repeated application of + and performs fewer
(virtual) function applications for computing derivatives.  The
allocation and loop for the array are relatively cheap.

> Finally, is it better at this stage to use softmax or to specify probs[n] <- exp(eta[n])/sum(eta[n]) in transformed
> parameters section?  categorical_logit will be available in stan 2.0?

Use softmax.  It should be have exactly the same way
in 1.3, which just defines softmax that way.

In Stan 2 (which we hope to launch a beta for next week),
has custom derivatives for softmax, which will be much faster
and much less memory intense.  The issue with memory is that
Stan stores the whole expression tree for the log probability,
which can get big.  For instance, softmax does a lot of work
for each n because it needs to be normalized.

The categorical_logit that's part of 2.0 gets around that
problem AND has a custom derivative.  So it's much faster
and much less memory intensive.

We would've done this sooner if we'd known there were
so many multi-logit fitters out there.  We're trying to
optimize according to perceived demand.

- Bob

I estimated a model in which the prior for the 3-way interactions were
allowed to have a different std dev than the other model terms (the
previous version treated all beta as being drawn from the same
distribution).  I allowed stan to fit what this standard deviation was
using a hyperprior.

This worked much better.  It took about 45 minutes with 3 processors and
produced a minimum effective sample size of 115; the first quartile was
over 1,200.

It may also be relevant that I changed the coding scheme to contr.sum so
that all the coefficients summed to zero (e.g., for the A*B interaction
the sum of the coefficients for each combination of levels was zero).

The prior for the lower order beta had a median sd of 0.08 and for the
3-way terms an sd of 0.002!

So, all the 3 way interactions are trivial (the posteriors are what
you'd expect from such a tight prior).

This is another example of estimation improving by allowing an sd to be
fit, in this case as an extremely small value.  Conversely, another
example of convergence problems with excessively diffuse priors.

I worry a little that if one of the 3-way interactions really were
important it might be dragged down by their general smallness.  I
suppose the model would not end up with such a tight prior if that were
the case.

Ross

>>> There are some things I don't think rstan does (using the development
>>> version, but perhaps the help files don't reflect all recent work) that
>>> I would like it to do.
>>>
>>> 1. extract() has options to include or exclude warmup.  It would be nice
>>> to have an option to specify the warmup period if, for example, I run
>>> 2,000 iterations (with the default half of them warmup) but decide that
>>> things seemed to have converged after fewer than 1,000 iterations.
>>
>>> Or is it not a good idea to use the warmup period, during which it is
>>> tuning parameters?
>>
>> Not a good idea.  The problem is that the warmup iterations
>> don't form a Markov chain, so none of our inferences from them
>> would be appropriate.
>
> I was somewhat generalizing from the monitor function which does let
> you specify the warmup period.  But it's good to know I shouldn't do
> that.

Yikes.  We need to fix that to prevent that.

I'll verify and open an issue in RStan.

> At least in principle some users are not autotuning and so might want
> more control.  I'm not one of those users.

We don't even know how to automatically tune convergence
yet.

> I'm also a little nervous about using anything but the default 1/2
> warmup period.  My concern is that some of the stanfit functions have
> the assumption that it is 1/2 wired in; I believe some of the help
> files are written that way.

I hope not.  Is there something specific that causes
problem if warmup is something other than half the iterations?

I haven't had any problems with the basic functions, but
I haven't explored the corners of RStan.

> I've been running chains of 2,000 iterations, and as far as I can tell
> convergence takes much less than 1,000 iterations.  So it's kind of
> wasteful.

It is indeed wasteful in some situations to use half for warmup.
Usually it's when you need a very large number of effective samples
but convergence is fast.

Be careful about concluding things about convergence by eye.
Stan continues to adapt during warmup and this can be helpful
for sampling speed.  So it can look from the traceplots like
you've converged, but spending some more time in warmup can help
with the number of effective samples/second during sampling.

Stan 2 is less wasteful of iterations in warmup, so specifying
a shorter warmup time should work better.  Stan 1.3 will throw
away the adaptation from some of the later adaptation stages if
the warmup isn't an even multiple of the adaptation windows.

>> We've been considering some kind of auto-tuning that can turn
>> off adaptation on its own, but we haven't really figured out how
>> to monitor the statistics we need efficiently as samples come in
>> or figured out a good methodology for stopping.
>>

I agree, but I'm not designing RStan at that level of detail.

>> Is that why you want (2) above, to

I find all of R gets stuck in my keyboard :-)

Nice!  I haven't even played with the development RStan yet.

Hi all,

I had some time to look into it, and I now have a diffusion model working in Stan. I was able to use much of the code in the JAGS module, which was nice. I've barely tested this at all, though, so... caveat emptor. The implementation requires three files, all available here: http://www.cidlab.com/supp.php?o=wienerstan
Put the files in the right location, overwrite where needed, remake Stan, now you have  ~wiener(a,t,b,v).

Joachim

messages.body_plain:
I use the following slightly awkward code to pull the *minimum* of the effective sample sizes from a stanfit object...

get_min_neff <- function(fit) {
  min({summary(fit)}$summary[, 'n_eff'])
}

Bob - feel free to modify / take as is / reject / etc...

Note this is the minimum across all constrained and unconstrained parameters and it is based on all chains... it'd be a bit more work to pull each individually... or the parameters individually...

I wanted to do marginal density plots across different datasets, so I wanted to try and make them approximately comparable, so I "optimized" for an n_eff of 500 +/- 10%...

Kind regards,
Sean

messages.subject: How can one add a quantty generated in the "model" step to generated quantities ?
messages.subject_clean: How can one add a quantty generated in the "model" step to generated quantities ?
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am trying to  duplicate Carlin & Chib (1995) results on the modelization of the compressive strength of Pines radiata wood by two linear regressio. This is easy to do. It is also easy to write Stan code that fits those two models in parallel. One can also easily get the log-posterior densities for each of these models (see attached code and data).

What I am not able to do is to add those log-posteriors in the output sample. If I declare them in the "parameters" or "transformed parameters" block, Stan detects an affectation in the wrong block ; if I declare them in the model block, they are no longer visible in the "generated quantities" block, and Stan tells me that these variable do not exist.

This seems to be a more general problem : one cannot (currently) get samples of anything else than parameters or expressions using them. Such a possibility might be useful for (in example) to sample other derived quantities of data and parameters (yes, I'm thinking *also* about DIC/WAIC... More on this in a further post, when ready).

I see two potential solutions to this problem :
1) extend the scope of the "model"variables to the "generated quantities" block ; or
2) create a special pseudo-distribution "ident" which would be a Dirac of its argument with unit mass. This would allow to declare such quantities as paraeters, thus allowing to sample them without violating current scope rules.

Am I missing something ?

                                                                   Emmanuel Charpentier

On 9/29/13 9:15 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier wrote:
> Dear list,
>
> I am trying to  duplicate Carlin & Chib (1995) results on the modelization of the compressive strength of Pines radiata
> wood by two linear regressio. This is easy to do. It is also easy to write Stan code that fits those two models in
> parallel. One can also easily get the log-posterior densities for each of these models (see attached code and data).
>
> What I am not able to do is to add those log-posteriors in the output sample. If I declare them in the "parameters" or
> "transformed parameters" block, Stan detects an affectation in the wrong block ; if I declare them in the model block,
> they are no longer visible in the "generated quantities" block, and Stan tells me that these variable do not exist.

You didn't include an example, but I'm guessing you're trying
to define a transformed parameter in the model block, which is
illegal.  You need to define transformed parameters in the
transformed parameter block.

> This seems to be a more general problem : one cannot (currently) get samples of anything else than parameters or
> expressions using them. Such a possibility might be useful for (in example) to sample other derived quantities of data
> and parameters (yes, I'm thinking *also* about DIC/WAIC... More on this in a further post, when ready).

Technically, the samples are just of the parameters.  And the
unconstrained parameters, at that.  Everything
else is derived from the parameters, including the constrained
parameters you see in the model.  You can use the data to
derive quantities in either transformed parameters or generated
quantities --- the data variables are available in all subsequent
blocks.

> I see two potential solutions to this problem :
> 1) extend the scope of the "model"variables to the "generated quantities" block ; or
> 2) create a special pseudo-distribution "ident" which would be a Dirac of its argument with unit mass. This would allow
> to declare such quantities as paraeters, thus allowing to sample them without violating current scope rules.
>
> Am I missing something ?

Solution 1 could work.  But if the variables have top-level
scope in the model block, you can declare them as transformed
parameters.  You just have to assign them values in the
transformed parameter block.  This was the way I intended this
kind of thing to be done.

Proposal 2 is both messy and difficult to implement in a general
HMC algorithm (it's possible by treating constraints the right way,
but we currently throw an error if you try to set a variable's
lower-bound and upper-bound constraint to the same value).

It's ugly in the modeling language, but it's actually more efficient
to just recompute in the generated quantities block.  Any quantity that
depends on a parameter (transformed parameter, local variable in model
block) creates an automatic differentiation variable (or several), which
have to be managed dynamically in memory and are the main bottleneck
in Stan's execution speed at the moment (and in any foreseeable future
where we need to compute derivatives).

It's always a shame when implementation details intrude on an
otherwise flexible modeling language.  Maybe one day we'll get more
clever in Stan program analysis and code generation so we can
optimize some of these issues away --- but we're a long way away from
thinking about this kind of thing.

- Bob
